hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that reduced glutathione reductase (GSR) activity exacerbates oxidative stress in Aminoacylase-1 deficiency by impairing the regeneration of reduced glutathione (GSH), due to accumulation of N-acetylated amino acids that competitively inhibit GSR. In Aminoacylase-1 deficiency, failure to hydrolyze N-acetyl-amino acids leads to their systemic buildup; certain N-acetyl-amino acids (e.g., N-acetylcysteine) may structurally mimic GSR substrates or allosteric regulators. We predict that pathophysiological concentrations of N-acetylcysteine directly inhibit GSR in vitro, decreasing NADPH-dependent GSSG reduction by ≥50% compared to controls. This would be confirmed by kinetic assays showing non-competitive inhibition of purified human GSR by N-acetylcysteine (K<0.1 mM), and refuted if no significant inhibition occurs (p>0.05, n=3) or if other N-acetyl-amino acids lacking thiol groups show equal inhibition. This mechanism would impair redox homeostasis, contributing to the neurological symptoms observed in Aminoacylase-1 deficiency.

We hypothesize that AKR1A1 exacerbates oxidative stress in ethylmalonic encephalopathy by reducing methylglyoxal to acetol, consuming NADPH and thereby limiting glutathione regeneration. In ethylmalonic encephalopathy, impaired short-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (SCAD) function leads to accumulation of ethylmalonic acid and secondary mitochondrial dysfunction, increasing reactive oxygen species (ROS) and methylglyoxal formation. AKR1A1, which catalyzes NADPH-dependent reduction of methylglyoxal, may deplete cytosolic NADPH pools needed for maintaining reduced glutathione, worsening redox imbalance. We predict that AKR1A1 knockdown in patient-derived fibroblasts will decrease acetol formation, increase NADPH and reduced glutathione levels, and reduce ROS compared to controls. Conversely, AKR1A1 overexpression will further deplete NADPH, increase oxidative damage, and impair cell viability. These outcomes would confirm AKR1A1’s role in redox disruption; absence of such effects would refute it.

We hypothesize that reduced activity of the mitochondrial complex I subunit NDUFA10 impairs NADH-dependent superoxide production in myeloid precursors, leading to diminished hydrogen peroxide availability required for myeloperoxidase (MPO) maturation and heme insertion. Since MPO depends on H₂O₂ to form the catalytically active ferryl heme intermediate during post-translational processing, chronic underproduction of mitochondrial superoxide due to NDUFA10 dysfunction may result in improperly processed, inactive MPO—mimicking genetic MPO deficiency. We predict that myeloid cells with NDUFA10 knockdown will show decreased complex I-driven ROS, reduced mature MPO protein, and impaired microbial killing—phenotypes rescued by exogenous H₂O₂ or mitochondrial-targeted superoxide generators. Conversely, normal MPO processing in NDUFA10-deficient cells would refute this mechanism. This hypothesis links mitochondrial redox signaling via a specific complex I subunit to MPO activation, offering a metabolic explanation for acquired MPO deficiency in contexts of mitochondrial dysfunction.

We hypothesize that PPIP5K2 modulates the accumulation of AICA-riboside in AICA-ribosuria due to ATIC deficiency by regulating the phosphorylation state of inositol pyrophosphates, which in turn influences AMPK activity and purine salvage pathway flux. Specifically, elevated AICA-riboside levels in ATIC deficiency may trigger energy stress, activating AMPK; PPIP5K2-generated 5-IP7 (a potent pyrophosphoryl donor) could inhibit AMPK via direct pyrophosphorylation, thereby disrupting feedback regulation of purine biosynthesis and exacerbating AICA-riboside excretion. We predict that PPIP5K2 knockout in ATIC-deficient human fibroblasts will reduce AICA-riboside accumulation by >50% (measured via LC-MS) due to sustained AMPK activation and downregulation of de novo purine synthesis. Conversely, PPIP5K2 overexpression will increase AICA-riboside excretion. This hypothesis is refuted if PPIP5K2 modulation shows no effect on AICA-riboside levels despite confirmed AMPK pyrophosphorylation changes.

We hypothesize that reduced activity of ribose-5-phosphate isomerase A (RPIA) impairs the non-oxidative pentose phosphate pathway (PPP), decreasing ribose-5-phosphate availability for nucleotide synthesis and increasing cytosolic oxidative stress due to imbalanced NADPH regeneration. In neurons with high metabolic demand, this exacerbates mitochondrial dysfunction in Leigh syndrome by limiting nucleotide pools required for mtDNA maintenance and repair, particularly in complex I-deficient cells. We predict that RPIA knockdown in patient-derived fibroblasts with SURF1 mutations will reduce mtDNA copy number and amplify respiratory chain deficiency, especially when challenged with oxidative stress. Conversely, RPIA overexpression will restore ribose-5-phosphate flux, improve mtDNA stability, and rescue oxygen consumption rates. This hypothesis is falsified if RPIA modulation shows no effect on mtDNA levels or bioenergetics in Leigh syndrome cells, despite confirmed PPP metabolite changes.

We hypothesize that reduced activity of the LIPT1 enzyme, which catalyzes the lipoylation of the E2 subunit of pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH), impairs mitochondrial energy metabolism and exacerbates lysosomal dysfunction in Mucopolysaccharidosis 7 (MPS 7), caused by β-glucuronidase deficiency. Accumulation of glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) in MPS 7 disrupts lysosomal pH, potentially impairing trafficking or stability of LIPT1, leading to decreased PDH activity and bioenergetic deficit. We predict that fibroblasts from MPS 7 patients will show reduced LIPT1 protein levels, diminished PDH lipoylation, and lower oxygen consumption rates compared to controls. Treating these cells with recombinant β-glucuronidase will restore LIPT1 function and PDH lipoylation, confirming the link. Conversely, if LIPT1 levels and lipoylation remain normal in MPS 7 cells, or if enzyme replacement fails to correct them despite GAG clearance, the hypothesis will be refuted.

We hypothesize that GNPNAT1, through its role in glucosamine-6-phosphate biosynthesis, indirectly disrupts coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10) production by impairing the hexosamine biosynthetic pathway (HBP)-dependent O-GlcNAcylation of key CoQ10 biosynthetic enzymes, such as COQ7, in primary CoQ10 deficiency, type 6. Reduced O-GlcNAc modification due to GNPNAT1 insufficiency may destabilize COQ7 or hinder its mitochondrial localization, contributing to CoQ10 deficiency. We predict that GNPNAT1 knockdown in human fibroblasts will reduce COQ7 O-GlcNAcylation, decrease CoQ10 levels, and impair respiratory chain function—effects reversible by glucosamine supplementation. Conversely, overexpression of GNPNAT1 should restore O-GlcNAcylation and CoQ10 biosynthesis. Detection of reduced O-GlcNAcylated COQ7 and low CoQ10 in GNPNAT1-deficient cells would support the hypothesis; absence of these changes, despite GNPNAT1 loss, would refute it. This mechanism specifically links GNPNAT1 to the pathophysiology of primary CoQ10 deficiency, type 6.

We hypothesize that loss-of-function mutations in *PTEN* (phosphatase and tensin homolog) lead to hyperactivation of the PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling pathway, which suppresses SREBP-2 processing and nuclear translocation, thereby downregulating transcription of *FDFT1*, the gene encoding squalene synthase. This transcriptional repression exacerbates the biochemical phenotype of squalene synthase deficiency by further reducing cholesterol biosynthesis flux, worsening endogenous cholesterol depletion. We predict that in patient-derived fibroblasts with squalene synthase deficiency, pharmacologic inhibition of AKT will restore SREBP-2 activity and increase squalene synthase expression and cholesterol synthesis rates. Conversely, constitutive PTEN loss in these cells will further diminish residual squalene synthase activity. This hypothesis is falsifiable: if AKT inhibition fails to upregulate squalene synthase expression or cholesterol synthesis in this context, the proposed mechanistic link is invalidated.

We hypothesize that dysfunction of the NDUFS1 subunit of mitochondrial Complex I impairs NAD⁺ regeneration, reducing the activity of NAD⁺-dependent dehydrogenases in lysine catabolism, specifically α-aminoadipic semialdehyde dehydrogenase, leading to accumulation of phosphohydroxylysine and causing phosphohydroxylysinuria. We propose that NDUFS1 deficiency-induced NADH buildup shifts the NAD⁺/NADH ratio, inhibiting NAD⁺-dependent steps upstream of phosphohydroxylysine metabolism. Prediction: Fibroblasts from phosphohydroxylysinuria patients with biallelic NDUFS1 mutations will show decreased NAD⁺/NADH ratios and reduced conversion of radiolabeled lysine to CO₂ and α-aminoadipate, which will be rescued by expression of wild-type NDUFS1. Conversely, absence of metabolic rescue or normal NAD⁺/NADH ratios in patient cells would refute this mechanism. This hypothesis links mitochondrial redox state directly to the metabolic block in phosphohydroxylysinuria via NDUFS1-specific dysfunction.

We hypothesize that reduced NDUFA5, a subunit of mitochondrial complex I, impairs NAD⁺ regeneration, exacerbating redox imbalance in Transaldolase deficiency. In this disorder, disrupted pentose phosphate pathway (PPP) flux leads to accumulation of sedoheptulose-7-phosphate and NADP⁺ depletion, limiting glutathione reduction. We propose that NDUFA5 dysfunction further compromises redox homeostasis by decreasing NAD⁺ availability for cytosolic NAD kinase, reducing NADP⁺ synthesis and thus NADPH production via the oxidative PPP. This dual hit on NADPH generation amplifies oxidative stress in Transaldolase deficiency. Prediction: In TAL-deficient human fibroblasts, siRNA knockdown of NDUFA5 will decrease NAD⁺/NADH and NADP⁺/NADPH ratios and increase ROS (confirmatory); conversely, NDUFA5 overexpression will restore ratios and reduce ROS (refutative if no change occurs). This interaction is testable via metabolomics and redox probes.

We hypothesize that reduced activity of glutaminase 2 (GLS2) in intestinal epithelial cells impairs glutamine-dependent anion secretion, contributing to the dehydration of meconium and the development of meconium ileus. GLS2 catalyzes mitochondrial glutamine hydrolysis to glutamate, supporting NADPH production and redox balance essential for cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR)-mediated chloride and bicarbonate secretion. In the context of CFTR dysfunction—central to meconium ileus—GLS2 insufficiency may further compromise luminal fluidity by diminishing substrate availability for anion transport. We predict that GLS2 knockdown in human fetal intestinal organoids will reduce glutamine-driven fluid secretion, exacerbating mucus viscosity, whereas GLS2 overexpression will partially rescue secretion. Confirmation: increased mucus hydration and anion flux with GLS2 upregulation. Refutation: no change or worsening of secretion despite GLS2 modulation.

We hypothesize that VNN2 (vanin-2) exacerbates oxidative stress in glutathione synthetase deficiency by depleting cellular cysteamine, a precursor for de novo glutathione synthesis. VNN2 hydrolyzes pantetheine into cysteamine and pantothenic acid; in glutathione synthetase deficiency, where glutathione regeneration is impaired, VNN2-mediated cysteamine production may be rapidly oxidized, limiting substrate availability for alternative antioxidant pathways. We predict that genetic knockout or pharmacological inhibition of VNN2 in patient-derived fibroblasts will increase intracellular cysteamine and partially restore redox balance, evidenced by increased total glutathione equivalents and reduced ROS levels under oxidative challenge. Conversely, overexpression of VNN2 will further deplete cysteamine and worsen redox imbalance. This hypothesis is falsifiable: if VNN2 inhibition fails to elevate cysteamine or improve redox status, or if effects are absent in cysteamine-supplemented cells, the proposed mechanism is invalidated.

terminal_shown: Cerebellar ataxia, deafness, and narcolepsy, autosomal dominant
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that mutations in NDUFB1, a subunit of mitochondrial complex I, impair electron transport chain efficiency specifically in auditory hair cells, cerebellar Purkinje neurons, and hypothalamic orexin-producing neurons, leading to chronic bioenergetic deficit and oxidative stress that underlie cerebellar ataxia, deafness, and narcolepsy in the autosomal dominant form of the disease. We propose that dominant-negative NDUFB1 mutations disrupt complex I assembly, reducing ATP synthesis and increasing superoxide production in these selectively vulnerable cell types. Prediction: In patient-derived neurons, we will observe decreased complex I activity, elevated ROS, and reduced orexin expression; these effects will be rescued by wild-type NDUFB1 expression. Refutation: If NDUFB1 mutations show no impact on complex I function or if mitochondrial deficits are absent in affected neurons, the hypothesis is invalidated.

We hypothesize that deficiency in α-galactosidase A (GLA), the lysosomal enzyme defective in Fabry disease, leads to infantile-onset limb and orofacial dyskinesia via accumulation of globotriaosylceramide (Gb3) in basal ganglia neurons, disrupting calcium homeostasis and impairing GABAergic neurotransmission. Specifically, Gb3 accumulation in striatal medium spiny neurons induces lysosomal membrane permeabilization, releasing cathepsins that cleave vesicular GABA transporter (vGAT), reducing synaptic GABA levels. This disinhibits thalamocortical circuits, manifesting as hyperkinetic movements. We predict that GLA-knockout mice will exhibit orofacial and limb dyskinesias beginning in infancy, accompanied by reduced vGAT and elevated extracellular GABA in the striatum, measurable via microdialysis and immunoblotting. These symptoms and biochemical changes will be prevented by early gene therapy–mediated GLA expression in the striatum. Conversely, absence of striatal vGAT reduction or lack of dyskinesia in GLA-knockout mice would refute this hypothesis.

terminal_shown: Neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly, movement abnormalities, and seizures
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that ALAS1 deficiency in developing neurons impairs mitochondrial heme synthesis, leading to reduced cytochrome c activity, diminished oxidative phosphorylation, and chronic bioenergetic stress that disrupts cortical neurogenesis and synaptic function, thereby contributing to neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly, movement abnormalities, and seizures. Specifically, ALAS1 loss-of-function decreases heme availability in neural progenitor cells, triggering cell cycle arrest and premature differentiation via AMPK activation and mTORC1 inhibition. We predict that conditional knockout of ALAS1 in murine neural progenitors will result in microcephaly, seizure-like activity, and motor deficits, accompanied by reduced brain heme levels and respiratory chain dysfunction. These phenotypes would be rescued by neuron-specific expression of wild-type ALAS1 but not catalytically inactive ALAS1 (K313A), confirming the metabolic dependence on ALAS1-derived heme. Absence of such deficits would refute the hypothesis.

We hypothesize that PRKACA, the catalytic alpha subunit of protein kinase A, disrupts Hedgehog (Hh) signaling in limb development by aberrantly phosphorylating GLI transcription factors, contributing to Temtamy preaxial brachydactyly syndrome. Specifically, hyperactivation of PRKACA leads to inhibitory phosphorylation of GLI2/3, reducing expression of downstream targets such as *PTCH1* and *SHH*, which are critical for anterior-posterior digit patterning. We predict that in patient-derived mesenchymal cells with *CA8* mutations (linked to Temtamy syndrome), elevated PRKACA activity correlates with increased GLI3 repressor formation and reduced SHH signaling. This would be confirmed by detecting higher phospho-GLI3 (Ser856) and lower *SHH* target gene expression via immunoblotting and qPCR; refuted if GLI3 phosphorylation and SHH signaling remain unchanged despite PRKACA inhibition. This mechanism directly links cAMP/PKA overactivity to the preaxial brachydactyly phenotype.

We hypothesize that SPHK2 (sphingosine kinase 2) promotes mitochondrial dysfunction in cardiomyocytes by elevating intramitochondrial sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P), thereby contributing to the pathogenesis of dilated cardiomyopathy, 1GG (DCM1GG). In DCM1GG, mutations in the TAZ gene impair cardiolipin remodeling, destabilizing mitochondrial inner membrane structure. We propose that SPHK2 translocates to the mitochondria under stress and generates S1P locally, which binds to and inhibits electron transport chain complex III, exacerbating oxidative phosphorylation defects in TAZ-deficient cardiomyocytes. Prediction: Genetic ablation of SPHK2 in TAZ-deficient human iPSC-derived cardiomyocytes will restore complex III activity, reduce mitochondrial ROS, and improve contractile function. Conversely, SPHK2 overexpression will worsen these phenotypes. This hypothesis is falsifiable by measuring mitochondrial respiration and S1P levels in SPHK2-modulated, TAZ-mutant cardiomyocytes.

We hypothesize that ETHE1 deficiency impairs mitochondrial sulfide detoxification, leading to toxic hydrogen sulfide (H₂S) accumulation that disrupts lysyl hydroxylase (PLOD1) activity in connective tissue fibroblasts, thereby reducing collagen cross-linking in Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, kyphoscoliotic type 1. H₂S can inhibit Fe²⁺-dependent dioxygenases like PLOD1 by binding their catalytic iron, and ETHE1 is essential for H₂S oxidation in mitochondria. In ETHE1-deficient cells, elevated H₂S levels would impair PLOD1-mediated hydroxylation of lysine residues in collagen, mimicking the collagen defects seen in PLOD1-mutant patients. We predict that fibroblasts from ETHE1-deficient models will show reduced PLOD1 activity and abnormal collagen cross-links, which are rescued by scavenging H₂S (e.g., with sulfide quinone oxidoreductase overexpression). Conversely, failure to restore PLOD1 function despite H₂S reduction would refute this mechanism. This hypothesis links ETHE1’s biochemical role to the hallmark collagen pathology of kyphoscoliotic Ehlers-Danlos syndrome via H₂S-mediated enzyme inhibition.

We hypothesize that SOS1 (Son of Sevenless 1) exacerbates porphyria-related encephalopathy by amplifying ERK/MAPK signaling in response to heme deficiency, thereby increasing neuronal excitotoxicity and oxidative stress. During acute porphyria attacks, heme depletion upregulates ALAS1, leading to accumulation of neurotoxic porphyrin precursors. We propose that heme deficiency activates SOS1-mediated RAS-ERK signaling in astrocytes and neurons, promoting glutamate dysregulation and mitochondrial dysfunction. Specifically, SOS1 activation increases phosphorylation of ERK1/2, which downregulates astrocytic glutamate transporter EAAT2, elevating synaptic glutamate and contributing to encephalopathy. We predict that SOS1 knockdown or inhibition in neuronal-glial co-cultures exposed to 5-aminolevulinic acid (ALA) and low heme will prevent ERK overactivation, restore EAAT2 expression, reduce glutamate levels, and improve neuronal survival. Conversely, SOS1 overexpression under these conditions should worsen outcomes. Genetic or pharmacologic SOS1 inhibition in a murine model of acute intermittent porphyria should reduce seizure incidence and cognitive deficits, confirming the hypothesis; lack of effect would refute it.

terminal_shown: Vertebral, cardiac, renal, and limb defects syndrome 2
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that mutations in *CERK* (ceramide kinase) disrupt sphingolipid signaling during embryonic development, contributing to Vertebral, cardiac, renal, and limb defects syndrome 2 (VLCRD2). Specifically, loss-of-function mutations in *CERK* reduce production of ceramide-1-phosphate (C1P), impairing PI3K/Akt signaling and downstream regulation of mesodermal patterning and cell survival in developing somites, heart fields, nephrogenic cords, and limb buds. Given that VLCRD2 is linked to dysregulated embryonic morphogenesis and *CERK* is expressed in these tissues during critical windows, we propose that C1P deficiency leads to aberrant apoptosis and defective epithelial-mesenchymal transitions. Prediction: *Cerk*-knockout mice will exhibit vertebral fusions, cardiac outflow tract malformations, renal agenesis, and limb reductions; these defects will be rescued by embryonic administration of cell-permeable C1P. Failure to phenocopy key features of VLCRD2 or lack of rescue would refute the hypothesis.

We hypothesize that mutations in the mitochondrial tyrosyl-tRNA synthetase YARS2 impair mitochondrial protein synthesis, reducing the abundance of functional carbamoyl phosphate synthetase 1 (CPS1), the rate-limiting enzyme of the urea cycle. Specifically, YARS2 deficiency may compromise translation of mitochondrial-encoded subunits of respiratory chain complexes, leading to secondary mitochondrial dysfunction, decreased ATP production, and insufficient energy supply for CPS1 activity, which requires two ATP molecules per catalytic cycle. This bioenergetic deficit would exacerbate hyperammonemia in individuals with partial CPS1 deficiency. We predict that fibroblasts from patients with YARS2 mutations will show reduced CPS1 enzyme activity under high-ammonia challenge, reversible by ATP supplementation or expression of wild-type YARS2. Conversely, no rescue will occur if CPS1 deficiency is due to primary CPS1 mutations under the same conditions. This hypothesis links YARS2-dependent mitochondrial translation to CPS1 function via bioenergetics, offering a testable mechanism for phenotypic modulation in CPS1 deficiency.

We hypothesize that asparagine synthetase (ASNS) deficiency impairs N-linked glycosylation of α-dystroglycan by limiting asparagine availability for dolichol-linked oligosaccharide precursor synthesis, exacerbating the pathogenesis of muscular dystrophy-dystroglycanopathy limb-girdle type C7 (MDDGC7), which arises from defective glycosyltransferase-like domain-containing protein 1 (GTDC1)-mediated O-mannosylation. Reduced ASNS activity decreases the asparagine pool required for the Asn-X-Ser/Thr motif glycosylation initiation, leading to hypoglycosylated α-dystroglycan and disrupted dystrophin-glycoprotein complex integrity in skeletal muscle. We predict that ASNS overexpression in MDDGC7 patient-derived myotubes will restore α-dystroglycan glycosylation and laminin binding, confirming the hypothesis; conversely, ASNS knockdown in control myotubes will phenocopy the glycosylation defect. This prediction is falsified if modulating ASNS expression fails to alter α-dystroglycan glycosylation status despite functional GTDC1 expression.

We hypothesize that ARAF kinase modulates the phosphorylation state of phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH), influencing its catalytic activity and stability in hepatocytes. Specifically, we propose that aberrant ARAF activation leads to inhibitory phosphorylation of PAH at Ser13, reducing its ability to convert phenylalanine to tyrosine, thereby exacerbating hyperphenylalaninemia in PAH deficiency. This mechanism operates independently of PAH mutations but worsens residual enzyme function in hypomorphic variants. We predict that genetic knockdown or pharmacological inhibition of ARAF in a PAH-deficient hepatocyte model (e.g., HepG2 cells expressing mutant PAH) will increase PAH activity, reduce intracellular phenylalanine levels, and enhance PAH protein stability. Conversely, ARAF overexpression will further suppress PAH function. These effects should be absent in PAH-null systems, confirming dependence on residual PAH expression. Confirmation requires measurement of PAH activity and phenylalanine clearance; refutation occurs if ARAF modulation shows no effect on PAH function or phenylalanine metabolism.

We hypothesize that ENTPD2, by hydrolyzing extracellular ATP to ADP, modulates purinergic signaling that indirectly regulates pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) complex activity via P2Y1 receptor–mediated intracellular Ca²⁺ flux. In Pyruvate dehydrogenase E1-alpha deficiency, reduced PDH activity leads to metabolic reliance on glycolysis and increased ATP release. Chronic ENTPD2 upregulation in this context may exacerbate PDH suppression by sustaining ADP-dependent P2Y1 activation, which promotes Ca²⁺-mediated activation of pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase (PDK), leading to inhibitory phosphorylation of residual PDH E1-alpha. We predict that ENTPD2 inhibition or knockout will reduce PDK activation, decrease PDH E1-alpha phosphorylation, and increase PDH activity in patient-derived fibroblasts, improving oxidative metabolism. Conversely, ENTPD2 overexpression should worsen PDH suppression. This hypothesis is falsified if ENTPD2 modulation shows no effect on PDH phosphorylation or activity in E1-alpha–deficient cells.

We hypothesize that sucrase-isomaltase (SI) contributes to non-cirrhotic portal hypertension through excessive fructose generation in the small intestine, leading to systemic absorption and hepatic fructokinase-dependent activation of de novo lipogenesis, oxidative stress, and sinusoidal endothelial dysfunction. Specifically, elevated SI activity increases luminal fructose from dietary starch and sucrose digestion, promoting portal fructose delivery. Chronic fructose metabolism in perivenous hepatocytes generates uric acid and reactive oxygen species, inducing sinusoidal inflammation and increased intrahepatic resistance without fibrosis. We predict that SI-knockdown in fructose-rich diet-fed wild-type mice will reduce hepatic oxidative stress markers (e.g., 4-HNE), lower portal pressure, and improve sinusoidal perfusion compared to controls. Conversely, absence of these effects despite SI reduction would refute the hypothesis. This mechanism aligns with known fructose metabolism and the metabolic endothelial phenotype in non-cirrhotic portal hypertension.

We hypothesize that AGA (aspartylglucosaminidase) deficiency exacerbates Congenital erythropoietic porphyria (CEP) by impairing lysosomal degradation of uroporphyrinogen I, leading to its accumulation and oxidation to uroporphyrin I in erythroid cells. AGA, though primarily associated with glycoasparagine catabolism, may indirectly influence porphyrin metabolism through lysosomal dysfunction, given its role in maintaining lysosomal integrity. In CEP, uroporphyrinogen III synthase deficiency causes uroporphyrinogen I accumulation; we propose that defective AGA-mediated lysosomal clearance further increases uroporphyrinogen I retention, promoting its non-enzymatic oxidation and subsequent phototoxic porphyrin deposition. Prediction: AGA-knockdown human erythroid progenitor cells will show increased intracellular uroporphyrin I levels compared to controls when exposed to aminolevulinic acid. Refutation: No significant change in uroporphyrin I accumulation in AGA-deficient cells would disprove this hypothesis.

We hypothesize that D-glucuronyl C5-epimerase (DGLUCY) deficiency impairs the epimerization of D-glucuronic acid to L-iduronic acid in the uronic acid pathway, leading to compensatory shunting of D-glucuronic acid into the polyol pathway where it is reduced to L-xylulose by aldose reductase. Inadequate further metabolism of L-xylulose due to low xylulokinase activity results in its accumulation and urinary excretion, manifesting as essential pentosuria. We predict that fibroblasts or hepatocytes from pentosuria patients will exhibit significantly reduced DGLUCY activity, elevated levels of intracellular L-xylulose, and increased flux of glucose into L-xylulose in isotopic tracer (e.g., [U-¹³C]-glucose) experiments. This hypothesis would be confirmed by these findings and refuted if DGLUCY activity is normal and L-xylulose accumulation persists independently of D-glucuronic acid buildup.

We hypothesize that HAO2 (hydroxyacid oxidase 2) modulates intracellular levels of 2-hydroxybutyrate, which competitively inhibits ITPA (inosine triphosphate pyrophosphohydrolase), exacerbating ITP accumulation in ITPA deficiency. Under physiological conditions, HAO2 metabolizes 2-hydroxybutyrate, a byproduct of cysteine biosynthesis. When HAO2 activity is reduced, 2-hydroxybutyrate accumulates and directly inhibits residual ITPA activity in individuals with partial loss-of-function ITPA variants, increasing ITP incorporation into RNA and promoting translational errors. We predict that HAO2 knockdown in ITPA-deficient human hepatocytes will increase 2-hydroxybutyrate levels, elevate ITP:ATP ratios, and impair protein synthesis fidelity—measured by ribosomal misreading of inosine-containing transcripts. Conversely, HAO2 overexpression or 2-hydroxybutyrate scavenging will restore ITPA function and reduce ITP accumulation. This hypothesis is refuted if 2-hydroxybutyrate shows no inhibition of ITPA in vitro or if HAO2 modulation fails to alter ITP levels in ITPA-deficient cells.

We hypothesize that deficient adenosine kinase (ADK) activity disrupts adenosine homeostasis in enteric glia, leading to adenosine-mediated excitotoxicity and impaired gut motility in visceral neuropathy, familial, 1, autosomal recessive (VNF1). In VNF1, mutations in *AGPAT6* may indirectly compromise ADK localization or stability in mitochondrial compartments of enteric nervous system cells, reducing adenosine phosphorylation to AMP. This elevates extracellular adenosine, overactivating A2B receptors on enteric neurons and glia, triggering chronic cAMP/PKA signaling, calcium dysregulation, and neuroinflammation. We predict that VNF1 patient-derived enteric neurons will exhibit reduced ADK enzymatic activity, elevated extracellular adenosine, and hyperactivation of A2B receptors—reversed by ADK overexpression or A2B antagonism. Conversely, normal adenosine metabolism and receptor signaling in these cells would refute the hypothesis. This mechanism links ADK dysfunction directly to VNF1’s neuropathic gastrointestinal phenotype via purinergic signaling dysregulation.

We hypothesize that HYI (4-hydroxy-2-oxoglutarate aldolase), which catalyzes the cleavage of 4-hydroxy-2-oxoglutarate into pyruvate and glyoxylate in the hydroxyproline degradation pathway, exacerbates metabolic toxicity in 3-ketothiolase deficiency (caused by mutations in *ACAT1*) by increasing glyoxylate availability. Accumulated glyoxylate may be oxidized to oxalate, promoting oxalate crystal deposition and renal damage—complications observed in some patients. In 3-ketothiolase deficiency, impaired isoleucine catabolism leads to buildup of intermediates like (S)-3-hydroxy-2-methylbutyryl-CoA, which may divert metabolism toward alternative pathways, increasing reliance on hydroxyproline degradation and thus HYI activity. We predict that *Acatt1*-deficient mice with *Hyi* knockout will show reduced urinary oxalate and improved renal histology compared to *Acatt1*-deficient mice with intact *Hyi*. Conversely, elevated oxalate in *Acatt1*;*Hyi* double-mutant models would refute this hypothesis. This leverages known substrate promiscuity and compartmentalization of mitochondrial metabolism.

We hypothesize that ATP6V1FP2, a subunit of the vacuolar H⁺-ATPase (V-ATPase) complex, impairs cholesterol trafficking in Smith-Lemli-Opitz syndrome (SLOS) by disrupting endolysosomal acidification, thereby exacerbating defective DHCR7-mediated cholesterol synthesis. In SLOS, reduced DHCR7 activity leads to cholesterol deficiency and toxic 7-dehydrocholesterol (7-DHC) accumulation. Proper endolysosomal acidification, dependent on ATP6V1FP2-containing V-ATPase complexes, is essential for LDL-derived cholesterol release and SREBP-2 activation. We propose that ATP6V1FP2 dysfunction further reduces cholesterol availability by impairing lysosomal cholesterol export, amplifying sterol regulatory defects. Prediction: In SLOS patient fibroblasts, knockdown of ATP6V1FP2 will reduce lysosomal acidification (measured by LysoTracker), decrease free cholesterol in the endoplasmic reticulum (detected by D4H staining), and increase 7-DHC accumulation (via GC-MS), compared to controls. Conversely, ATP6V1FP2 overexpression will partially restore acidification and cholesterol homeostasis. Failure to observe these changes would refute the hypothesis.

terminal_shown: Polycystic liver disease 3 with or without kidney cysts
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that BRCA1 dysfunction impairs DNA damage repair in cholangiocytes, leading to aberrant activation of the mTORC1 pathway via accumulation of genomic stress, thereby promoting cystogenesis in Polycystic Liver Disease 3 (PCLD3). Specifically, loss of BRCA1-mediated homologous recombination repair results in persistent DNA double-strand breaks, triggering ATM/ATR-dependent phosphorylation of TSC2 and consequent disinhibition of mTORC1. Hyperactive mTORC1 increases cell proliferation and fluid secretion in liver bile duct epithelia, driving cyst formation. We predict that liver-specific *Brca1* knockout mice with heterozygous mutations in *PRKCSH* (a PCLD3-associated gene) will develop significantly more hepatic cysts than controls. This would be confirmed by increased γH2AX and p-S6 immunostaining in cyst-lining cells; conversely, absence of cyst exacerbation or mTORC1 activation in double mutants would refute the hypothesis.

We hypothesize that B3GALT6, which catalyzes the formation of β1,3-galactosyltransferase linkages in proteoglycan biosynthesis, impairs glutathione synthetase (GSS) function through aberrant post-translational modification of membrane-associated transporters critical for cysteine uptake. Specifically, defective glycosylation of the xCT subunit of the system xc⁻ cystine/glutamate antiporter due to B3GALT6 dysfunction reduces cystine import, depleting intracellular cysteine—a rate-limiting substrate for glutathione synthesis. This exacerbates the metabolic defect in Glutathione synthetase deficiency, where GSS activity is already compromised. We predict that fibroblasts from GSS-deficient patients with concomitant B3GALT6 knockdown will show significantly lower reduced glutathione levels and heightened oxidative stress compared to controls, and that this effect will be rescued by cell-permeable cysteine esters. Conversely, if glutathione levels remain unchanged despite B3GALT6 suppression, the hypothesis will be refuted.

terminal_shown: Neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly, seizures, and cortical atrophy
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that loss-of-function mutations in ASAH1, which encodes acid ceramidase, impair ceramide degradation in lysosomes, leading to toxic accumulation of ceramides in neural progenitor cells. This disrupts lysosomal membrane integrity, triggers aberrant autophagy, and promotes caspase-dependent apoptosis during early cortical development. Consequently, reduced neuronal proliferation and premature cell death contribute to microcephaly, cortical atrophy, and hyperexcitable neural networks underlying seizures. Specifically, we predict that patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) neural progenitors with biallelic ASAH1 mutations will exhibit elevated C16- and C18-ceramide levels, lysosomal leakage (measured by cathepsin B mislocalization), increased LC3-II/p62 accumulation, and elevated caspase-3 cleavage compared to isogenic controls. CRISPR-mediated correction of the mutations will normalize these phenotypes, confirming causality. Conversely, absence of ceramide accumulation or rescue upon gene correction would refute this mechanism.

We hypothesize that mutations in phosphopantothenoylcysteine decarboxylase (PPCDC) cause Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy 89 (DEE89) by impairing coenzyme A (CoA) biosynthesis, leading to deficient mitochondrial acetyl-CoA production and disrupted neuronal energy metabolism. Specifically, loss-of-function PPCDC variants reduce decarboxylation of 4'-phospho-N-pantothenoylcysteine, causing intracellular CoA depletion. This disrupts the tricarboxylic acid cycle and acetyl-CoA-dependent processes, including neurotransmitter synthesis and histone acetylation, thereby impairing neurodevelopment and promoting hyperexcitability. We predict that patient-derived neurons with biallelic *PPCDC* mutations will show reduced CoA levels, diminished ATP production, and increased seizure-like activity in cortical organoids—phenotypes rescued by expression of wild-type PPCDC but not catalytically inactive mutants (e.g., D79A). Conversely, if CoA levels and neuronal activity are normal in these models, the hypothesis is refuted. This mechanism directly links PPCDC dysfunction to DEE89 pathogenesis via bioenergetic failure in developing neurons.

We hypothesize that loss-of-function mutations in H6PD, the hexose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase responsible for generating NADPH in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), impair redox homeostasis and disrupt protein folding in neurons, contributing to the pathogenesis of Spastic paraplegia 64 (SPG64). Specifically, H6PD deficiency reduces intraluminal NADPH, compromising the activity of ER-resident glutathione reductase and protein disulfide isomerases, leading to chronic ER stress and unfolded protein response activation in corticospinal motor neurons. This selective neuronal vulnerability results in axonal degeneration characteristic of SPG64. We predict that patient-derived SPG64 neurons with H6PD mutations will exhibit elevated ER stress markers (e.g., CHOP, phosphorylated eIF2α) and increased sensitivity to thapsigargin-induced ER stress, which would be rescued by targeted expression of wild-type H6PD. Failure to observe elevated ER stress or rescue with H6PD re-expression would refute this hypothesis.

We hypothesize that CSGALNACT2, a chondroitin sulfate N-acetylgalactosaminyltransferase, modulates peripheral nerve myelination by regulating glycosaminoglycan chain elongation on proteoglycans in Schwann cells, and that loss-of-function variants in CSGALNACT2 disrupt extracellular matrix integrity, contributing to axonal degeneration in Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, axonal, type 2N (CMT2N). Specifically, reduced CSGALNACT2 activity impairs chondroitin sulfate modification of key matrix proteoglycans (e.g., neurocan), destabilizing Schwann cell-axon interactions and impairing axonal support. We predict that CMT2N patient-derived Schwann cells with CSGALNACT2 mutations will exhibit shortened chondroitin sulfate chains and disrupted co-culture myelination with sensory neurons, which would be rescued by lentiviral CSGALNACT2 expression. Conversely, normal chain length and myelination in mutant cells would refute the hypothesis.

terminal_shown: Mitochondrial complex I deficiency, nuclear type 4
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that TMEM86A, a transmembrane protein of unknown biochemical function, regulates the assembly or stability of mitochondrial complex I by facilitating the mitochondrial import or membrane integration of NDUFS2, a nuclear-encoded subunit mutated in mitochondrial complex I deficiency, nuclear type 4 (MC1DN4). Specifically, we propose that TMEM86A interacts with the TIM22 complex to mediate the insertion of hydrophobic complex I subunits into the inner mitochondrial membrane. Loss-of-function mutations in TMEM86A would disrupt this process, leading to defective complex I assembly, reduced NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductase activity, and impaired oxidative phosphorylation. Prediction: siRNA knockdown of TMEM86A in human fibroblasts will reduce NDUFS2 protein levels, decrease complex I activity by ≥50% (measured spectrophotometrically), and impair mitochondrial respiration (measured via Seahorse assay). These defects would be rescued by wild-type TMEM86A, but not by a non-functional mutant. Failure to observe these effects would refute the hypothesis.

We hypothesize that loss-of-function mutations in the FHIT (Fragile Histidine Triad) enzyme lead to accumulation of its substrate, diadenosine tetraphosphate (Ap4A), resulting in aberrant activation of the MTH1 (NUDT1) hydrolase and dysregulated nucleotide pool balance in developing neurons. This imbalance impairs DNA repair and mitochondrial function, promoting neuronal hyperexcitability and neurodevelopmental deficits characteristic of Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy 71 (DEE71). Specifically, elevated Ap4A competes with ATP for mitochondrial RNA cap binding, disrupting mitochondrial transcript stability and oxidative phosphorylation. We predict that DEE71 patient-derived neurons with biallelic *FHIT* mutations will exhibit increased Ap4A levels, reduced mitochondrial respiration, and elevated seizure-like activity in multielectrode array assays—phenotypes reversible upon Ap4A scavenging or MTH1 inhibition. Conversely, absence of Ap4A accumulation or mitochondrial dysfunction in these neurons would refute the hypothesis.

terminal_shown: Triokinase and FMN cyclase deficiency syndrome
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that impaired function of the mitochondrial complex I subunit ND5 disrupts cellular redox balance, leading to reduced FAD availability and exacerbating metabolic dysfunction in Triokinase and FMN cyclase deficiency syndrome. Specifically, ND5 dysfunction decreases NAD⁺ regeneration, limiting the activity of FAD synthase—which requires FMN and ATP to produce FAD—by lowering the NAD⁺-dependent activity of enzymes that maintain ATP and FMN pools. This creates a pathogenic synergy: deficient FMN cyclase already limits FMN production, and impaired NAD⁺ metabolism further restricts FAD synthesis. We predict that patient-derived cells with ND5 mutations will show significantly reduced FAD levels and increased methylglyoxal accumulation (due to impaired glyoxalase system function), which will be partially rescued by NAD⁺ precursors. Conversely, no such rescue would refute the redox-dependent mechanism.

We hypothesize that glucokinase (GK), a key glycolytic enzyme regulating glucose phosphorylation in neurons and astrocytes, contributes to the pathogenesis of Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis 11 (ALS11) by disrupting hexosamine biosynthesis pathway (HBP) flux due to altered glucose metabolism. ALS11, caused by mutations in the *SIGMAR1* gene encoding sigma-1 receptor (Sig-1R), impairs ER-mitochondria Ca²⁺ signaling and proteostasis. We propose that dysfunctional Sig-1R leads to mislocalization of GK, reducing glucose entry into the HBP and diminishing O-GlcNAcylation of TDP-43, a post-translational modification that stabilizes the protein. Hypo-O-GlcNAcylation promotes TDP-43 hyperphosphorylation and cytoplasmic aggregation, a hallmark of ALS11. Prediction: In *SIGMAR1*-mutant motor neurons, GK inhibition will reduce O-GlcNAc levels and increase TDP-43 aggregation, while GK activation or HBP supplementation (e.g., glucosamine) will restore O-GlcNAcylation and reduce aggregates—effects absent if GK is knocked out.

We hypothesize that CDS1 (CDP-diacylglycerol synthase 1) promotes hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) progression by altering mitochondrial membrane phospholipid composition, leading to impaired electron transport chain (ETC) function and increased reactive oxygen species (ROS). Specifically, CDS1 upregulation in HCC cells increases CDP-diacylglycerol production, diverting phosphatidic acid from cardiolipin synthesis, a key mitochondrial phospholipid required for ETC complex stability. This results in defective oxidative phosphorylation, metabolic reprogramming toward glycolysis, and ROS-driven activation of HIF-1α and NF-κB signaling, enhancing tumor proliferation and survival. We predict that liver-specific CDS1 knockdown in a murine HCC model (e.g., diethylnitrosamine-induced) will restore cardiolipin levels, improve mitochondrial respiration, reduce tumor burden, and decrease proliferation markers (e.g., Ki-67). Conversely, CDS1 overexpression should exacerbate tumorigenesis. These outcomes would confirm the hypothesis; absence of metabolic or tumor changes despite CDS1 modulation would refute it.

We hypothesize that PLCG1 (phospholipase C gamma 1) dysregulation impairs peroxisomal import of ACSF3, the mitochondrial acyl-CoA synthetase essential for malonic acid detoxification, by disrupting phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2) dynamics at the peroxisomal membrane. In combined malonic and methylmalonic aciduria (CMAMMA), loss-of-function mutations in *ACSF3* lead to malonic and methylmalonic acid accumulation, but we propose that aberrant PLCG1 activity—through excessive PIP2 hydrolysis—compromises PEX5-dependent protein import, exacerbating ACSF3 deficiency even in patients with residual *ACSF3* function. Specifically, we predict that PLCG1 overexpression in patient-derived fibroblasts will reduce peroxisomal ACSF3 levels and increase malonic acid accumulation, whereas PLCG1 inhibition will restore ACSF3 import and normalize acid levels. This would confirm the hypothesis; conversely, no change in ACSF3 localization or metabolite levels upon PLCG1 modulation would refute it.

We hypothesize that loss of NDUFS4 function in mitochondrial complex I impairs oxidative phosphorylation, leading to increased mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mtROS) production in juvenile CD4+ T cells, which promotes a pro-inflammatory Th17 phenotype and exacerbates synovial inflammation in juvenile arthritis. Specifically, NDUFS4 deficiency reduces NAD+ regeneration, shifting cellular metabolism toward glycolysis and stabilizing HIF-1α, a known driver of IL-17 expression. We predict that conditional knockout of Ndufs4 in T cells of juvenile mice will increase Th17 differentiation and severity of collagen-induced arthritis, measurable by elevated IL-17A, synovitis, and joint erosion. This effect would be reversed by mtROS scavengers (e.g., MitoQ) or HIF-1α inhibition. Conversely, absence of increased Th17 responses or arthritis severity in Ndufs4-deficient mice would refute the hypothesis. This mechanism directly links mitochondrial dysfunction via a specific enzyme to immune dysregulation in juvenile arthritis.

terminal_shown: Mitochondrial complex I deficiency, nuclear type 7
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that HIBADH (3-hydroxyisobutyrate dehydrogenase) deficiency impairs mitochondrial NAD⁺ regeneration in valine catabolism, exacerbating redox stress in mitochondrial complex I deficiency, nuclear type 7 (caused by mutations in NDUFAF5). HIBADH converts 3-hydroxyisobutyrate to methylmalonate semialdehyde, generating NADH in mitochondria. In NDUFAF5-deficient cells, where complex I assembly and NADH oxidation are already compromised, reduced HIBADH activity would further elevate the NADH/NAD⁺ ratio, intensifying electron leakage and oxidative damage. Conversely, HIBADH upregulation may partially compensate by sustaining NAD⁺ flux through alternative dehydrogenases. We predict that HIBADH knockdown in NDUFAF5-mutant fibroblasts will decrease NAD⁺/NADH ratio, increase superoxide production, and worsen respiration defects—confirming the hypothesis. Conversely, if HIBADH modulation shows no effect on NAD⁺ homeostasis or respiration in NDUFAF5-deficient cells, the hypothesis is refuted. This mechanism specifically links valine catabolism to redox imbalance in nuclear-encoded complex I deficiency.

We hypothesize that ACER3 deficiency disrupts sphingolipid homeostasis in epidermal keratinocytes by impairing the deacylation of phytoceramide into phytosphingosine, leading to toxic accumulation of N-acyl-ethanolamine-phosphoethanolamine (PEA-PE) derivatives and defective cornified envelope formation, thereby driving the hyperkeratosis and erythematous patches characteristic of Erythrokeratodermia variabilis et progressiva 4 (EKVP4). Specifically, loss-of-function mutations in ACER3 reduce phytosphingosine regeneration, perturbing ceramide:phospholipid ratios essential for lamellar body secretion and stratum corneum integrity. We predict that ACER3-knockdown human keratinocytes will exhibit elevated PEA-PE and abnormal tight junction permeability, which can be rescued by exogenous phytosphingosine — confirming the hypothesis. Conversely, absence of lipid abnormalities or lack of phytosphingosine rescue would refute it. This mechanism aligns with EKVP4’s genetic association with *ACER3* mutations and known sphingolipid roles in skin barrier function.

We hypothesize that JAG1, a ligand in the Notch signaling pathway, modulates the expression of *SGSH* (encoding N-sulfoglucosamine sulfohydrolase), the enzyme deficient in Mucopolysaccharidosis 3A (MPS IIIA). Specifically, we propose that reduced JAG1-mediated Notch signaling in neural progenitor cells downregulates *SGSH* transcription, exacerbating heparan sulfate accumulation in the central nervous system. This dysregulation occurs via impaired cleavage and nuclear translocation of the Notch intracellular domain (NICD), diminishing its activation of *SGSH* promoter elements. We predict that conditional knockout of *Jag1* in murine neural precursors will reduce *Sgsh* mRNA and increase heparan sulfate levels, phenocopying neuropathology in MPS IIIA mice—confirming the hypothesis. Conversely, if *Jag1* deletion does not alter *Sgsh* expression or glycosaminoglycan accumulation, the hypothesis is refuted. This mechanism links developmental signaling to lysosomal enzyme regulation, offering a novel pathway influencing MPS IIIA severity.

We hypothesize that TOP2A dysfunction in neuronal nuclei leads to unresolved DNA topological stress during transcription of long, axonally transported mRNAs essential for motor neuron integrity, contributing to Neuronopathy, distal hereditary motor, X-linked. Specifically, impaired TOP2A-mediated relaxation of supercoiled DNA in motor neurons increases R-loop accumulation and transcription-replication conflicts, causing DNA damage and aberrant splicing of genes critical for distal axonal function. Because this X-linked disorder predominantly affects motor neurons with long axons, we predict that patient-derived motor neurons will exhibit elevated DNA double-strand breaks and mis-splicing of genes such as *MFN2* and *HSPB1*, which are implicated in axonal transport and mitochondrial dynamics. This hypothesis is falsifiable: confirmation would require demonstration of reduced TOP2A activity correlating with R-loop accumulation and splicing defects in patient neurons; refutation would occur if TOP2A inhibition fails to recapitulate these molecular phenotypes or if pathology persists despite TOP2A overexpression.

terminal_shown: Mitochondrial complex I deficiency, nuclear type 4
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that loss-of-function mutations in the MTM1-encoded myotubularin phosphatase disrupt phosphoinositide (PI) homeostasis, leading to aberrant mitochondrial fission via impaired recruitment of dynamin-related protein 1 (Drp1) to mitochondria, thereby contributing to Mitochondrial complex I deficiency, nuclear type 4. Specifically, MTM1 dephosphorylates phosphatidylinositol 3-phosphate (PI3P) and PI(3,5)P2; its deficiency may elevate these lipids on endosomal and mitochondrial-associated membranes, disrupting membrane dynamics required for proper complex I assembly. We predict that MTM1-knockdown cells will show increased mitochondrial PI3P, fragmented mitochondria, reduced Drp1 translocation, and decreased complex I activity—rescuable by expression of wild-type MTM1 but not catalytically inactive MTM1-C375S. Conversely, if MTM1 deficiency does not alter mitochondrial phosphoinositide levels or complex I assembly independently of Drp1 mislocalization, the hypothesis is refuted. This links MTM1’s lipid phosphatase activity directly to the pathogenesis of nuclear-encoded complex I deficiency via organelle dynamics.

We hypothesize that pyruvate carboxylase (PC) deficiency impairs aspartate synthesis in neurons by reducing oxaloacetate production in the mitochondria, thereby disrupting the malate-aspartate shuttle and limiting neuronal NAD+ regeneration. In Spastic paraplegia 26 (SPG26), caused by recessive mutations in *CYP2U1*, defective fatty acid metabolism leads to accumulation of neurotoxic metabolites that increase mitochondrial oxidative stress. We propose that PC activity is further compromised under these conditions, exacerbating aspartate deficiency and impairing axonal energy metabolism in corticospinal motor neurons. Prediction: SPG26 patient-derived neurons will show reduced aspartate levels and diminished PC activity, which will be rescued by CYP2U1 re-expression or aspartate supplementation but not by antioxidants alone. Conversely, if aspartate levels are normal or PC activity is unaffected in SPG26 models, the hypothesis is refuted. This links PC dysfunction to SPG26 via metabolic crosstalk between fatty acid oxidation and anaplerotic metabolism.

We hypothesize that thymidylate synthase (TYMS) deficiency leads to imbalanced dNTP pools in peripheral nerve cells, impairing mitochondrial DNA replication and repair in Schwann cells, thereby contributing to axonal degeneration in Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, dominant intermediate C (CMTDIC). This disease is caused by mutations in the *DNM2* gene, which regulates endosomal trafficking and mitochondrial dynamics. We propose that TYMS dysfunction exacerbates *DNM2*-related mitochondrial defects by limiting dTTP availability, increasing mtDNA instability, and amplifying oxidative stress. Prediction: In *DNM2*-mutant Schwann cell models, pharmacologic or genetic inhibition of TYMS will reduce mtDNA copy number and increase fragmentation (confirmatory), whereas TYMS overexpression or dTTP supplementation will restore mtDNA levels and mitochondrial morphology (refuting if no rescue occurs). These outcomes would establish a metabolic vulnerability linking nucleotide metabolism to CMTDIC pathogenesis.

We hypothesize that phosphatidylethanolamine N-methyltransferase (PEMT) deficiency disrupts mitochondrial membrane phospholipid composition in neurons, exacerbating the pathogenesis of Spastic paraplegia 39 (SPG39), caused by recessive mutations in the *CYP2U1* gene. CYP2U1 metabolizes polyunsaturated fatty acids critical for maintaining mitochondrial integrity, and PEMT-mediated synthesis of phosphatidylcholine from phosphatidylethanolamine is essential for mitochondrial membrane dynamics. Impaired PEMT activity reduces mitochondrial phosphatidylcholine, leading to defective fusion/fission and axonal transport in long corticospinal neurons. We predict that *CYP2U1*−/− neurons with concomitant PEMT knockdown will exhibit worsened mitochondrial fragmentation and reduced anterograde transport versus *CYP2U1*−/− alone, measurable by live imaging of mitochondrial motility in differentiated iPSC-derived motor neurons. Conversely, overexpression of PEMT will rescue these defects. Failure to observe mitochondrial or transport abnormalities upon PEMT modulation would refute this hypothesis.

We hypothesize that CYP2A13 contributes to Lenz-Majewski hyperostotic dwarfism by aberrantly metabolizing all-trans retinoic acid in developing bone tissue, exacerbating dysregulated osteoblast differentiation driven by gain-of-function mutations in PTDSS1. Normally expressed in respiratory epithelium, ectopic CYP2A13 expression in skeletal progenitor cells—potentially induced by mutant PTDSS1-associated membrane stress—could accelerate retinoic acid clearance, disrupting retinoid signaling gradients essential for craniofacial and long bone morphogenesis. This disruption would amplify the hyperostotic and dysmorphic skeletal phenotypes characteristic of the disease. We predict that immunohistochemistry and single-cell RNA-seq of patient-derived cranial osteoblasts will detect ectopic CYP2A13 expression, and that CYP2A13 inhibition will restore retinoic acid levels and normalize osteoblast mineralization in vitro. Conversely, absence of CYP2A13 expression in patient cells or no effect of CYP2A13 inhibition on mineralization would refute this hypothesis.

We hypothesize that fibroblast growth factor 2 (FGF2) exacerbates leukoencephalopathy in porphyria-related disease by inducing heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1) overexpression in cerebral endothelial cells, leading to increased free iron and oxidative stress in white matter. In porphyria, impaired heme synthesis causes accumulation of neurotoxic porphyrin precursors; we propose FGF2 signaling via FGFR1 activates the ERK/Nrf2 pathway, upregulating HO-1 and accelerating heme catabolism, further disrupting iron homeostasis. This mechanism selectively damages oligodendrocytes and myelin in the central nervous system. Prediction: In a murine model of acute intermittent porphyria, genetic ablation of Fgf2 will reduce HO-1 induction, decrease white matter iron deposition, and ameliorate MRI-detectable leukoencephalopathy compared to wild-type controls. Conversely, exogenous FGF2 administration will worsen leukoencephalopathy. Refutation would occur if Fgf2 knockout fails to reduce HO-1 activity or white matter injury despite porphyrin accumulation.

We hypothesize that GGCT (gamma-glutamyl cyclotransferase) exacerbates metabolic dysfunction in 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA lyase (HL) deficiency by impairing glutathione salvage, leading to accumulation of gamma-glutamyl-amino acids that competitively inhibit residual HL enzyme activity. Under oxidative stress, increased glutathione turnover elevates gamma-glutamyl metabolites, which structurally resemble the gamma-glutamyl moiety of HMG-CoA; we propose these metabolites bind HL’s active site, further reducing its already compromised ability to cleave HMG-CoA into acetoacetate and acetyl-CoA. Prediction: In fibroblasts from HL-deficient patients, pharmacologic inhibition of GGCT will decrease gamma-glutamyl-amino acid levels and increase HMG-CoA lyase activity (measured via [14C]-leucine oxidation to CO2), whereas GGCT overexpression will further suppress activity. Refutation: If GGCT modulation alters metabolite levels but does not affect HMG-CoA lyase activity, the competitive inhibition mechanism is invalid. This mechanism specifically links redox metabolism to the pathophysiology of HL deficiency.

We hypothesize that loss-of-function mutations in CYP2R1, the primary hepatic 25-hydroxylase responsible for converting vitamin D3 to 25-hydroxyvitamin D [25(OH)D], lead to chronically low circulating 25(OH)D levels during infancy, impairing vitamin D-dependent neurodevelopmental processes in the basal ganglia and brainstem. Specifically, deficient vitamin D signaling disrupts dopamine receptor expression and GABAergic interneuron maturation, increasing susceptibility to infantile-onset limb and orofacial dyskinesia. We predict that infants with biallelic pathogenic CYP2R1 mutations will exhibit significantly lower serum 25(OH)D and a higher incidence of early-onset dyskinesia compared to age-matched controls with normal CYP2R1 function. This hypothesis would be confirmed by observing dyskinesia in Cyp2r1-knockout mice with concomitant dopaminergic dysregulation in striatal circuits, preventable by neonatal 25(OH)D3 supplementation. It would be refuted if CYP2R1-deficient individuals maintain normal 25(OH)D levels and show no increased dyskinesia risk.

We hypothesize that IDO2 exacerbates inflammation in platelet-activating factor acetylhydrolase (PAFAH) deficiency by amplifying kynurenine pathway activation under oxidative stress, thereby increasing aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR) signaling and suppressing paraoxonase 1 (PON1) expression—a key stabilizer of PAFAH activity. In PAFAH deficiency, reduced hydrolysis of pro-inflammatory platelet-activating factor (PAF) and oxidized phospholipids leads to chronic inflammation; we propose that IDO2-derived kynurenine metabolites further impair residual PAFAH function via AhR-mediated transcriptional repression of PON1. This creates a feed-forward loop of inflammation and enzyme dysfunction. Prediction: In *Ido2* / *Pafah* double-knockout mice, we will observe higher PON1 levels and reduced plasma PAF compared to *Pafah*-deficient controls (confirming the hypothesis). Conversely, no significant difference in PAF hydrolysis or PON1 expression will refute it.

We hypothesize that AGPAT1, acylglycerol-3-phosphate acyltransferase 1, exacerbates lysosomal dysfunction in aspartylglucosaminuria by altering phosphatidic acid metabolism, thereby impairing autophagic flux secondary to defective lysosomal membrane composition. In aspartylglucosaminuria, deficiency of aspartylglucosaminidase leads to accumulation of glycoasparagines, which disrupt lysosomal pH and enzyme trafficking. We propose that accumulated substrates indirectly upregulate AGPAT1 activity, increasing phosphatidic acid synthesis and promoting aberrant lysosomal membrane curvature, which compromises autophagosome-lysosome fusion. Specifically, we predict that AGPAT1 knockdown in aspartylglucosaminuria patient-derived fibroblasts will restore autophagic clearance and reduce glycoasparagine storage, measurable by decreased LysoTracker fluorescence and reduced oligosaccharide accumulation via mass spectrometry. Conversely, AGPAT1 overexpression will worsen storage and autophagy defects. This hypothesis is falsifiable: if AGPAT1 inhibition fails to improve autophagic flux or substrate accumulation, the proposed mechanistic link is invalidated.

We hypothesize that ACSS3 deficiency impairs mitochondrial acetyl-CoA synthesis from acetate, disrupting the acetylation of key metabolic enzymes involved in phosphate homeostasis, thereby contributing to hyperphosphatemia in familial tumoral calcinosis, hyperphosphatemic, familial, 3 (TCFT3). Specifically, loss of ACSS3-mediated acetylation may dysregulate FGF23 post-translational modification or secretion in osteocytes, reducing circulating intact FGF23 and impairing renal phosphate excretion. We predict that ACSS3-knockout mice will exhibit decreased FGF23 acetylation, reduced serum intact FGF23, hyperphosphatemia, and ectopic calcifications—phenotypes rescued by osteocyte-specific ACSS3 re-expression. Conversely, if ACSS3 loss does not alter FGF23 processing or phosphate levels in this model, the hypothesis is refuted. This mechanism directly links mitochondrial acetate metabolism via ACSS3 to the FGF23-dependent phosphate dysregulation central to TCFT3.

terminal_shown: Mitochondrial complex IV deficiency, nuclear type 3
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that PLPP4 (pyridoxal phosphatase 4) deficiency impairs mitochondrial complex IV activity in nuclear type 3 deficiency by disrupting pyridoxal 5′-phosphate (PLP) homeostasis, thereby reducing the availability of heme A, a critical cofactor for complex IV assembly. PLPP4 dephosphorylates PLP to pyridoxal, regulating intracellular PLP levels; excess PLP inhibits ferrochelatase, the terminal enzyme in heme biosynthesis. We predict that PLPP4 loss-of-function increases mitochondrial PLP, inhibiting ferrochelatase and decreasing heme A synthesis, leading to defective complex IV. This hypothesis is confirmed if fibroblasts from patients with nuclear type 3 deficiency and reduced PLPP4 activity show elevated mitochondrial PLP, decreased heme A, and impaired complex IV assembly—rescued by PLPP4 re-expression or PLP-lowering agents. It is refuted if heme A levels and ferrochelatase activity remain normal despite PLPP4 deficiency, or if PLP modulation fails to alter complex IV function.

terminal_shown: Myopathy, mitochondrial progressive, with congenital cataract, hearing loss and developmental delay
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that mutations in glucokinase (GCK) impair glucose sensing in pancreatic beta cells and extra-pancreatic tissues, leading to chronic hypoglycemia, which secondarily reduces mitochondrial substrate availability in muscle, lens, cochlea, and developing brain. Sustained energy deficiency in these tissues diminishes ATP production, increases reactive oxygen species, and disrupts developmental metabolic signaling, contributing to mitochondrial dysfunction in myopathy, congenital cataract, sensorineural hearing loss, and developmental delay. Specifically, we predict that GCK loss-of-function mutations correlate with decreased glucose-stimulated insulin secretion and chronically low blood glucose, which in turn associate with reduced pyruvate-driven respiration in patient-derived skeletal muscle fibers. This hypothesis would be confirmed by demonstrating impaired oxidative phosphorylation in muscle mitochondria during low-glucose conditions in GCK-mutant patients, and refuted if mitochondrial function remains normal despite documented hypoglycemia.

We hypothesize that loss-of-function mutations in the cystathionine gamma-lyase (CTH) enzyme impair hydrogen sulfide (H₂S) production, disrupting redox homeostasis and mitochondrial bioenergetics in developing neurons, thereby contributing to the pathogenesis of Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy 84 (DEE84). Specifically, reduced CTH-derived H₂S diminishes sulfhydration of NMDAR and Kv7 channels, leading to neuronal hyperexcitability and impaired synaptic maturation. We predict that patient-derived neurons with biallelic CTH mutations will exhibit decreased H₂S levels, increased oxidative stress markers (e.g., 8-OHdG), and hyperexcitable network activity on multi-electrode arrays—phenotypes reversible with NaHS (H₂S donor) treatment. Conversely, if H₂S supplementation fails to normalize redox state and electrophysiological defects, the hypothesis is refuted. This mechanism aligns with known H₂S neuromodulatory roles and the early-onset seizures and developmental delay characteristic of DEE84.

We hypothesize that fructokinase (FCSK) indirectly exacerbates sulfatide accumulation in metachromatic leukodystrophy by depleting intracellular phosphate pools in renal and hepatic cells, impairing ATP-dependent steps in sphingolipid degradation. FCSK phosphorylates fructose using ATP, generating fructose-1-phosphate and inorganic phosphate (Pi) as a byproduct; however, chronic fructose metabolism can lead to transient phosphate sequestration, reducing Pi availability for ATP regeneration. Since arylsulfatase A (ASA), the deficient enzyme in metachromatic leukodystrophy, requires ATP-dependent post-translational modification (sulfation of its formylglycine residue) for full activity, FCSK-mediated phosphate fluctuations may further reduce residual ASA activity in partial deficiency states. We predict that FCSK knockout in ASA-deficient human fibroblasts will increase intracellular Pi and ATP, enhance ASA maturation, and reduce sulfatide accumulation compared to controls. Conversely, fructose supplementation will worsen sulfatide storage. This would confirm a metabolic modifier role for FCSK; absence of these effects would refute it.

We hypothesize that MTOR hyperactivation disrupts the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) localization or stability of the DOLK-encoded dolichol kinase, impairing dolichol-phosphate biosynthesis—a critical lipid carrier for N-glycosylation—thereby contributing to the pathogenesis of Congenital Disorder of Glycosylation 2T (CDG2T), caused by DOLK mutations. MTORC1 signaling regulates ER membrane dynamics and lipid synthesis; excessive MTOR activity may exacerbate DOLK deficiency by altering dolichol metabolism or mislocalizing residual DOLK enzyme. We predict that pharmacologic inhibition of MTOR (e.g., with rapamycin) in CDG2T patient fibroblasts will restore dolichol-phosphate levels and improve N-glycosylation efficiency, as measured by increased mature transferrin isoforms and reduced LLO intermediates. Conversely, MTOR activation will worsen glycosylation defects. This hypothesis is falsifiable: if MTOR inhibition fails to improve glycosylation or dolichol-phosphate levels in DOLK-deficient cells, the proposed mechanistic link is invalidated.

We hypothesize that tumor necrosis factor (TNF) disrupts neuronal migration during cortical development by aberrantly activating the RhoA/ROCK signaling pathway in neural progenitor cells, contributing to bilateral temporooccipital polymicrogyria. TNF, through TNFR1, may induce prolonged RhoA activation via RhoGEF phosphorylation, leading to excessive actin cytoskeleton stabilization and impaired nuclear translocation (nucleokinesis) in migrating neurons. This would manifest as overfolding and disorganized cortical lamination characteristic of polymicrogyria. We predict that in a fetal mouse model exposed to TNF overexpression, immunohistochemistry will reveal elevated phospho-ROCK and F-actin accumulation in the temporooccipital cortical plate, with corresponding microgyria-like malformations (confirmation). Conversely, if TNFR1 knockout or ROCK inhibition (e.g., fasudil) normalizes neuronal migration and cortical folding despite TNF exposure, the hypothesis is refuted. These experiments are feasible using in utero electroporation and ex vivo brain slice imaging.

We hypothesize that phosphoseryl-tRNA kinase (PSTK) deficiency impairs selenocysteine biosynthesis by reducing phosphorylation of seryl-tRNA[Ser]Sec, leading to diminished activity of glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4), a selenoenzyme critical for preventing lipid peroxidation in dopaminergic neurons. In Parkinson disease, this deficiency exacerbates ferroptotic cell death in the substantia nigra due to accumulated oxidative damage. We predict that postmortem brain tissue from Parkinson disease patients will show reduced PSTK expression correlated with decreased GPX4 levels and elevated lipid peroxidation markers (e.g., 4-HNE). Experimentally, knocking down PSTK in dopaminergic neuronal cell lines or mouse models will increase susceptibility to ferroptosis and worsen motor deficits, while PSTK overexpression or selenocysteine supplementation will rescue these phenotypes. Conversely, if PSTK modulation shows no effect on GPX4 activity or ferroptosis markers in dopaminergic neurons, the hypothesis will be refuted.

We hypothesize that kynurenine 3-monooxygenase (KMO) exacerbates metabolic stress in medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency (MCADD) by increasing NADPH consumption during hepatic kynurenine metabolism, thereby impairing NADPH-dependent recovery of glutathione and reducing antioxidant capacity during fasting-induced metabolic crisis. In MCADD, impaired fatty acid oxidation increases reliance on alternative energy pathways, elevating oxidative stress. KMO activity diverts NADPH to kynurenine oxidation, limiting availability for glutathione reductase. We predict that *Kmo* knockout in a Mcad-deficient mouse model will show reduced hepatic oxidative damage (measured by 4-HNE levels) and improved survival during fasting compared to *Kmo*-wildtype/Mcad-deficient controls. Conversely, overexpression of hepatic KMO will worsen outcomes. This prediction is falsifiable: if *Kmo* deletion fails to reduce oxidative stress or improve survival, the hypothesis is refuted. The mechanism specifically links KMO-driven redox imbalance to metabolic vulnerability in MCADD.

We hypothesize that ALOX15B exacerbates oxidative stress in Ethylmalonic encephalopathy by oxidizing membrane phospholipids containing arachidonic acid, leading to increased production of neurotoxic 15-HETE and lipid peroxidation products in the brain. In Ethylmalonic encephalopathy, impaired short-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (SCAD) function causes ethylmalonic acid accumulation and mitochondrial dysfunction, weakening antioxidant defenses. We propose that ALOX15B activity is upregulated under these conditions, amplifying neuronal damage through localized lipid peroxidation and inflammation. Inhibition of ALOX15B will reduce 15-HETE levels, lipid peroxidation markers (e.g., 4-HNE), and neuroinflammation in patient-derived neuronal cells or *Ethe1*-deficient mouse models. This hypothesis is falsifiable: if ALOX15B inhibition fails to reduce oxidative damage or improve mitochondrial function in these models, the proposed pathogenic role is unsupported. The prediction is testable via targeted lipidomics and functional assays following genetic knockdown or pharmacological inhibition of ALOX15B.

We hypothesize that impaired ALDH2 activity exacerbates oxidative stress in isolated sulfite oxidase deficiency by failing to detoxify reactive aldehydes generated during sulfite-induced lipid peroxidation. In this disease, sulfite accumulation promotes reactive oxygen species (ROS) formation, leading to membrane lipid peroxidation and production of toxic aldehydes such as 4-hydroxynonenal (4-HNE). ALDH2, a mitochondrial enzyme, normally metabolizes 4-HNE; however, under sustained sulfite exposure, ALDH2 may become inhibited or overwhelmed, resulting in aldehyde accumulation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and neuronal damage—key features of sulfite oxidase deficiency. We predict that ALDH2 activators (e.g., Alda-1) will reduce 4-HNE levels and improve cell viability in fibroblasts from sulfite oxidase-deficient patients exposed to sulfite. Conversely, ALDH2 inhibition or knockdown will worsen cytotoxicity. This hypothesis is falsifiable: if Alda-1 fails to reduce 4-HNE or improve outcomes in this context, the proposed protective role of ALDH2 is not supported.

We hypothesize that impaired activity of methionine synthase (MTR) disrupts the methionine cycle in retinal photoreceptors, leading to aberrant DNA methylation patterns that dysregulate the expression of *RP17*-associated genes such as *CRX* or *MAK*, ultimately triggering photoreceptor degeneration in Retinitis pigmentosa 17 (RP17). Specifically, MTR deficiency reduces S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) levels, diminishing methylation of CpG islands in promoters of photoreceptor maintenance genes. We predict that RP17 patient-derived retinal organoids with *RP17*-causing mutations will exhibit reduced MTR activity, decreased SAM:SAH ratios, and hypomethylation at key regulatory loci—reversible by MTR overexpression. Conversely, normal methylation and function in the same organoids with wild-type *MTR* expression would refute a causal role for MTR dysfunction in this context.

We hypothesize that reduced NAMPT activity exacerbates mitochondrial dysfunction in ethylmalonic encephalopathy (EE) by limiting NAD⁺ availability, thereby impairing SIRT3-dependent deacetylation of short-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (SCAD). In EE, caused by ETHE1 mutations, hydrogen sulfide (H₂S) accumulates, inhibiting mitochondrial complex IV and SCAD, leading to ethylmalonic acid accumulation. NAMPT, the rate-limiting enzyme in the NAD⁺ salvage pathway, sustains NAD⁺ levels required for SIRT3 activity. We predict that NAMPT upregulation will restore SIRT3-mediated SCAD activation, reduce ethylmalonic acid, and improve respiration in ETHE1-deficient fibroblasts. Conversely, NAMPT inhibition will worsen these phenotypes. This hypothesis is falsifiable: if NAMPT activation fails to increase NAD⁺, enhance SCAD activity, or reduce ethylmalonic acid in EE patient cells, the proposed mechanism is invalidated. The link integrates NAD⁺ metabolism with H₂S toxicity and SCAD dysfunction specific to EE.

We hypothesize that UGT2B11 modulates the detoxification and elimination of 7-dehydrocholesterol (7-DHC) derivatives in Smith-Lemli-Opitz syndrome (SLOS) by glucuronidating oxysterol byproducts such as 7-DHC-derived 3β,5α-dihydroxycholest-7-en-6-one (DHCEO), thereby reducing their cytotoxicity. In SLOS, defective DHCR7 leads to toxic accumulation of 7-DHC and its oxidation products, which contribute to oxidative stress and developmental defects. We propose that UGT2B11, expressed in liver and extrahepatic tissues, conjugates these reactive oxysterols, enhancing their solubility and excretion. We predict that overexpression of UGT2B11 in SLOS patient-derived fibroblasts will decrease intracellular levels of toxic 7-DHC oxysterols and reduce markers of oxidative stress (e.g., 4-HNE), while CRISPR-mediated knockout of UGT2B11 will exacerbate them. Confirmation would be demonstrated by LC-MS quantification of reduced glucuronidated DHCEO and elevated oxysterols in knockout cells; refutation would occur if no such changes are observed despite UGT2B11 modulation.

terminal_shown: Severe combined immunodeficiency autosomal recessive T-cell-negative/B-cell-negative/NK-cell-negative due to adenosine deaminase deficiency
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that CYP1B1 metabolizes adenosine or deoxyadenosine into reactive intermediates that exacerbate dATP accumulation in adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency, thereby intensifying inhibition of ribonucleotide reductase and impairing lymphocyte development in severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID). Specifically, CYP1B1-mediated oxidation may generate cytotoxic adenosine derivatives in thymic epithelial or hematopoietic cells, amplifying DNA replication stress and apoptosis in developing T, B, and NK cells. We predict that *CYP1B1 knockout in an ADA-deficient humanized mouse model will show improved lymphocyte counts and reduced dATP levels compared to ADA-deficient controls with functional CYP1B1*. Conversely, overexpression of CYP1B1 in ADA-deficient hematopoietic stem cells will worsen lymphopenia. This hypothesis is falsifiable: if CYP1B1 ablation does not alleviate immunodeficiency or dATP accumulation in ADA deficiency, the proposed pathogenic role is invalidated.

We hypothesize that purine nucleoside phosphorylase (PNP) deficiency leads to Combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency 12 (COXPD12) via impaired mitochondrial nucleotide salvage. PNP catalyzes the phosphorolysis of deoxyguanosine to guanine and deoxyribose-1-phosphate, a critical step in purine recycling. In PNP deficiency, deoxyguanosine accumulates and is phosphorylated to dGTP, which inhibits ribonucleotide reductase, depleting dNTP pools required for mtDNA replication. Given that COXPD12 is caused by mutations in *TRMT5*, encoding a mitochondrial tRNA methyltransferase essential for mitochondrial translation, we propose that PNP dysfunction exacerbates TRMT5-related defects by limiting dNTP availability, impairing mtDNA maintenance and amplifying respiratory chain deficiencies. We predict that fibroblasts from COXPD12 patients with concomitant PNP inhibition will show reduced mtDNA copy number and decreased Complex I and IV activity versus controls. Repletion of deoxyribonucleosides should rescue mtDNA levels; failure to do so would refute the hypothesis.

We hypothesize that COQ3, via its role in coenzyme Q (CoQ) biosynthesis, modulates mitochondrial oxidative stress in HPRT-deficient cells, thereby influencing purine degradation and uric acid overproduction in HPRT-related hyperuricemia. Specifically, COQ3 catalyzes O-methylation steps in CoQ10 synthesis, and its deficiency or inhibition exacerbates mitochondrial dysfunction, increasing ROS-driven xanthine oxidase activity and purine catabolism. In HPRT-deficient cells, which already exhibit purine recycling defects, reduced COQ3 activity further elevates uric acid production. We predict that siRNA-mediated knockdown of COQ3 in HPRT-deficient human renal tubular cells will increase mitochondrial ROS, xanthine oxidase activity, and extracellular uric acid levels compared to controls. Conversely, COQ3 overexpression or CoQ10 supplementation will normalize these parameters. This hypothesis is falsifiable: if COQ3 knockdown does not increase uric acid in HPRT-deficient cells, or if effects are independent of mitochondrial ROS, the proposed mechanism is invalidated.
