terminal_shown: Muscular dystrophy-dystroglycanopathy congenital with impaired intellectual development B14
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that HSD11B1, by locally amplifying glucocorticoids in skeletal muscle and brain, exacerbates endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress in *POMGNT1*-deficient cells, thereby worsening the hypoglycosylation of α-dystroglycan in Muscular dystrophy-dystroglycanopathy congenital with impaired intellectual development B14 (MDDGB14). Glucocorticoid overactivation via HSD11B1 impairs ER folding capacity, which may further disrupt the already compromised O-mannosyl glycosylation pathway due to *POMGNT1* mutations. We predict that pharmacological inhibition or genetic knockdown of HSD11B1 in *POMGNT1*-mutant patient-derived myotubes and neurons will reduce ER stress markers (e.g., CHOP, BiP), improve α-dystroglycan glycosylation (detected by IIH6 antibody), and restore laminin binding. Conversely, HSD11B1 overexpression will worsen glycosylation defects. These results would confirm a pathogenic role for HSD11B1; absence of improvement upon inhibition would refute it.

We hypothesize that gain-of-function mutations in the GNAS-encoded stimulatory G protein alpha subunit (Gαs) lead to Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy 84 (DEE84) by constitutively overactivating adenylyl cyclase, resulting in elevated neuronal cAMP levels, aberrant PKA signaling, and dysregulated synaptic plasticity. Specifically, hyperactive Gαs disrupts excitatory/inhibitory balance during critical neurodevelopmental periods by enhancing glutamatergic transmission and impairing GABAergic interneuron function. We predict that patient-derived neurons with GNAS mutations will exhibit increased cAMP production and hyperphosphorylation of the GluA1 subunit of AMPA receptors; pharmacological inhibition of adenylyl cyclase or PKA will normalize these signaling abnormalities and restore synaptic balance. Conversely, absence of cAMP/PKA dysregulation in patient neurons would refute this mechanism. This hypothesis integrates established Gαs-cAMP-PKA biochemistry with DEE84’s core phenotypes—early-onset seizures and neurodevelopmental impairment—providing a testable pathway specific to this disorder.

We hypothesize that NUDT13 modulates mitochondrial CoA ester homeostasis by hydrolyzing cytotoxic short/branched-chain acyl-CoA intermediates (e.g., isobutyryl-CoA, 2-methylbutyryl-CoA) that accumulate in short/branched-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency (SBCADD). In SBCADD, impaired dehydrogenase activity leads to buildup of these acyl-CoAs, disrupting mitochondrial metabolism. NUDT13, localized in mitochondria and known to hydrolyze acyl-CoA esters, may act as a compensatory detoxification enzyme by converting excess acyl-CoAs to their corresponding acyl phosphates and free CoASH, thereby mitigating CoA sequestration and restoring metabolic flux. We predict that NUDT13 knockout in SBCADD patient-derived fibroblasts will exacerbate acyl-CoA accumulation, reduce free CoASH, and impair fatty acid oxidation, while NUDT13 overexpression will ameliorate these effects. Conversely, if NUDT13 does not alter acyl-CoA levels or CoASH recovery in this context, the hypothesis will be refuted.

We hypothesize that CYP2J2-derived epoxyeicosatrienoic acids (EETs) protect against pathological vascular smooth muscle cell (VSMC) osteogenic transformation in arterial calcification of infancy, generalized, 1 (ACI1), a disease caused by loss-of-function mutations in ENPP1. Reduced ENPP1 activity decreases extracellular pyrophosphate (PPi), promoting hydroxyapatite deposition. CYP2J2, expressed in endothelial and vascular smooth muscle cells, metabolizes arachidonic acid to EETs, which we propose upregulate TNAP (tissue-nonspecific alkaline phosphatase) inhibitors and enhance KLF4-mediated maintenance of VSMC contractile phenotype. In ACI1, diminished CYP2J2 activity or EET bioavailability would exacerbate calcification due to unchecked TNAP activity and VSMC dedifferentiation. Prediction: In *Enpp1*-deficient infant aortic VSMCs, pharmacological activation of CYP2J2 or exogenous 14,15-EET will reduce calcium deposition and *Alpl* expression; conversely, CYP2J2 inhibition will worsen calcification. Refutation: No change or increased calcification with EET treatment.

We hypothesize that ALOX12B, a lipoxygenase catalyzing the oxidation of polyunsaturated fatty acids to hydroperoxy derivatives, exacerbates lipid peroxidation in mitochondrial membranes under conditions of impaired fatty acid β-oxidation due to mutations in HADHA, the alpha subunit of mitochondrial trifunctional protein (MTP), leading to secondary mitochondrial dysfunction in MTP deficiency type 1. Specifically, accumulation of long-chain fatty acid substrates in MTP deficiency increases ALOX12B-mediated production of 12(S)-HpETE, promoting oxidative stress and disrupting electron transport chain integrity. We predict that genetic knockdown or pharmacological inhibition of ALOX12B in patient-derived fibroblasts will reduce lipid peroxidation markers (e.g., 4-HNE) and improve mitochondrial respiration (measured by Seahorse assay). Conversely, overexpression of ALOX12B will worsen these parameters. This hypothesis is falsifiable: if ALOX12B inhibition fails to reduce oxidative stress or improve bioenergetics, the proposed mechanistic link is unsupported.

We hypothesize that impaired KARS1 activity reduces mitochondrial translation efficiency, decreasing the synthesis of glutamate formiminotransferase (encoded by *FTCD*), thereby exacerbating the metabolic phenotype of glutamate formiminotransferase deficiency. KARS1 charges mitochondrial tRNA^Lys with lysine, essential for oxidative phosphorylation complex synthesis; its dysfunction may indirectly limit the import or stability of nuclear-encoded FTCD by disrupting mitochondrial proteostasis and energy supply required for protein folding and trafficking. We predict that fibroblasts from patients with *KARS1* mutations will show reduced FTCD protein levels and formiminoglutamate (FIGLU) accumulation upon histidine loading, compared to controls—confirming the hypothesis. Conversely, normal FTCD levels and FIGLU excretion in *KARS1*-mutant cells would refute it. This mechanism links mitochondrial aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase function directly to the expressivity of an inborn error of folate metabolism.

We hypothesize that ENTPD8 deficiency impairs mitochondrial purine nucleotide catabolism, leading to accumulation of adenosine diphosphate (ADP) in the mitochondrial matrix, which allosterically inhibits methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (MUT) and malonyl-CoA decarboxylase (MLYCD). This dual inhibition disrupts both propionyl-CoA and malonyl-CoA metabolism, causing the characteristic combined malonic and methylmalonic aciduria (CMAMMA). Specifically, elevated ADP competes with the MUT cofactor adenosylcobalamin for binding sites, while inhibiting MLYCD activity required for malonate clearance. We predict that ENTPD8-knockout cells will exhibit increased mitochondrial ADP, reduced MUT and MLYCD activities, and elevated malonic and methylmalonic acid levels—phenotypes reversible by ectopic ENTPD8 expression or mitochondrial ADP scavenging. Conversely, absence of these metabolic changes in ENTPD8-deficient models would refute the hypothesis. This mechanism links nucleotide metabolism directly to CMAMMA pathogenesis via ENTPD8’s role in regulating mitochondrial ADP.

We hypothesize that thyroid peroxidase (TPO) dysfunction indirectly contributes to Erythrocytosis, familial, 8 (ECYT8), caused by gain-of-function mutations in the erythropoietin receptor (EPOR), via altered thyroid hormone signaling that modulates EPOR expression or JAK2/STAT5 pathway sensitivity. Specifically, reduced TPO activity leads to diminished thyroxine (T4) synthesis, lowering triiodothyronine (T3) levels, which in turn dysregulates erythroid progenitor responsiveness to erythropoietin. We predict that TPO-knockout mice crossed with ECYT8-EPOR mutant mice will exhibit exacerbated erythrocytosis compared to ECYT8 mice with normal TPO, due to compensatory erythropoietin elevation and enhanced JAK2/STAT5 activation in a hypothyroid state. Conversely, normalizing thyroid hormone levels in TPO-deficient ECYT8 mice will attenuate erythrocytosis. Exacerbation of red cell mass in the double-mutant mice would support the hypothesis; absence of such an effect would refute it.

We hypothesize that mutations in the mitochondrial complex I subunit ND1 impair electron transport chain efficiency, leading to increased mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mtROS) production in synovial tissue, which activates the NLRP3 inflammasome and drives IL-1β-mediated joint inflammation in Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis (JIA). Specifically, ND1 dysfunction alters complex I redox activity, promoting superoxide leakage that triggers oxidative stress and pro-inflammatory signaling in juvenile chondrocytes and synoviocytes. We predict that JIA patient-derived cells with pathogenic ND1 variants will exhibit elevated mtROS, increased NLRP3 activation, and heightened IL-1β secretion compared to controls—effects that will be reversed by mitochondrial-targeted antioxidants (e.g., MitoQ). Conversely, absence of elevated mtROS or inflammasome activation in ND1-variant cells would refute this mechanism. This hypothesis links a defined mitochondrial enzyme defect to JIA pathogenesis via a testable oxidative-inflammasome axis.

We hypothesize that CYP4F3, an enzyme responsible for ω-hydroxylation of very long-chain fatty acids (VLCFAs), modulates lipid homeostasis in peripheral nerve axons, and its dysfunction exacerbates axonal degeneration in Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, axonal, type 2D (CMT2D), caused by dominant mutations in *GARS1* (encoding glycyl-tRNA synthetase). Misfolded GARS1 may impair CYP4F3 expression or activity in Schwann cells or neurons, leading to VLCFA accumulation, disrupted myelin membrane integrity, and impaired axonal transport. We predict that *in vitro*, siRNA-mediated knockdown of CYP4F3 in dorsal root ganglion neurons expressing mutant GARS1 will increase intracellular VLCFAs and worsen mitochondrial trafficking deficits compared to controls. Conversely, CYP4F3 overexpression will normalize VLCFA levels and rescue trafficking. Confirmation: VLCFA accumulation and worsened trafficking upon CYP4F3 loss. Refutation: no change in VLCFAs or axonal transport despite CYP4F3 modulation.

We hypothesize that CYP4F8, an enzyme involved in the ω-hydroxylation of arachidonic acid and inactivation of anti-inflammatory epoxyeicosatrienoic acids (EETs), modulates cochlear inflammation and oxidative stress in the inner ear, contributing to the pathogenesis of Deafness, autosomal recessive, 44 (DFNB44), which is caused by mutations in the *TMHS* gene. Impaired CYP4F8 activity leads to dysregulated EET levels, exacerbating inflammation and hair cell dysfunction in the organ of Corti. We predict that *Cyp4f8* knockout mice crossed with *Tmhs* −/− mice will exhibit accelerated hearing loss and increased cochlear expression of pro-inflammatory markers (e.g., TNF-α, IL-6) compared to *Tmhs* −/− controls. Conversely, overexpression of CYP4F8 in *Tmhs* −/− mice will attenuate hearing loss and reduce oxidative stress. These outcomes would confirm the hypothesis; absence of such effects would refute it. This mechanism specifically links CYP4F8-mediated eicosanoid metabolism to DFNB44 pathology.

We hypothesize that CYP3A5 contributes to the pathogenesis of Primary Hyperoxaluria Type 2 (PH2) by metabolizing hydroxyproline or a related substrate into glyoxylate in hepatocytes, thereby increasing substrate availability for oxalate production. In PH2, deficient glyoxylate reductase/hydroxypyruvate reductase (GRHPR) activity already impairs glyoxylate detoxification; elevated glyoxylate generation via CYP3A5 could exacerbate oxalate accumulation. We predict that CYP3A5 overexpression in human hepatoma cells (e.g., HepG2) will increase glyoxylate and oxalate production from hydroxyproline, and that CYP3A5 inhibition (e.g., by ketoconazole) or siRNA knockdown will reduce glyoxylate/oxalate levels. Conversely, absence of such changes upon CYP3A5 modulation would refute its role. This mechanism specifically impacts PH2 by amplifying the metabolic flux through a compromised pathway, worsening endogenous oxalate overproduction unique to this disease.

We hypothesize that deficiency in dihydrolipoamide S-succinyltransferase (DLST), a component of the alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex, impairs mitochondrial alpha-ketoglutarate metabolism, leading to accumulation of glyoxylate and subsequent diversion of UDP-galactose to aberrant glycoconjugate synthesis, thereby disrupting Golgi-associated protein glycosylation in Congenital Disorder of Glycosylation 2T (CDG2T). Specifically, we propose that DLST dysfunction reduces succinyl-CoA production, altering the mitochondrial redox state and promoting glyoxylate-mediated depletion of UDP-galactose, a substrate for glycosyltransferases affected in CDG2T. Prediction: In DLST-deficient patient fibroblasts, we will observe decreased UDP-galactose levels, increased glyoxylate, and incomplete galactosylation of transferrin—biochemical hallmarks of CDG2T. These defects will be rescued by glyoxylate scavengers (e.g., phenylbutyrate) but not by galactose supplementation alone. Failure to observe these metabolic changes or correction with scavengers would refute the hypothesis.

We hypothesize that HSD17B7 deficiency, in combination with mutations in a second gene (e.g., *DHCR7*), disrupts cholesterol biosynthesis by impairing the C-17 reductase step in the Bloch pathway, leading to toxic accumulation of sterol intermediates that compromise embryonic development in AMED syndrome. Specifically, loss of HSD17B7 activity reduces conversion of zymosterone to zymosterol, causing buildup of methylated sterol precursors that impair membrane integrity and Hedgehog signaling. We predict that fibroblasts from digenic patients (HSD17B7 + DHCR7 variants) will show elevated zymosterone and reduced zymosterol/cholesterol ratios via mass spectrometry, and that these abnormalities will be rescued by wild-type HSD17B7 expression. Conversely, absence of these sterol alterations in patient cells would refute the hypothesis. This mechanism aligns with known sterol biochemistry and the digenic threshold model of AMED syndrome.

We hypothesize that CYP11A1, by catalyzing the initial step in steroidogenesis—cholesterol side-chain cleavage to pregnenolone—diverts cholesterol from mitochondrial membranes in skeletal muscle, impairing membrane integrity and electron transport chain (ETC) stability. In Recurrent myoglobinuria mitochondrial, this depletion exacerbates pre-existing mitochondrial dysfunction, increasing reactive oxygen species (ROS) production during metabolic stress, leading to rhabdomyolysis and myoglobinuria. We predict that muscle-specific CYP11A1 overexpression in a mouse model with partial ETC deficiency (e.g., *Bcs1l* mutation) will trigger exercise-induced myoglobinuria and worsened ETC dysfunction versus controls. Conversely, muscle-specific *Cyp11a1* knockout in the same model will reduce myoglobinuria episodes and ROS levels post-exercise. These outcomes would confirm or refute CYP11A1-mediated cholesterol shunting as a metabolic stress amplifier in this disease.

We hypothesize that AKT3 deficiency impairs osteoblast differentiation via dysregulation of mTORC1 signaling, contributing to the skeletal defects in Spondyloocular syndrome. Specifically, loss-of-function mutations in *XYLT2*, causative for Spondyloocular syndrome, reduce proteoglycan biosynthesis and extracellular matrix integrity, leading to diminished integrin-mediated activation of AKT3. We propose that reduced AKT3 activity in skeletal progenitor cells fails to phosphorylate and inhibit PRAS40, resulting in sustained suppression of mTORC1 and consequent downregulation of RUNX2, a master regulator of osteogenesis. This pathway links defective glycosaminoglycan assembly to impaired bone mineralization. Prediction: In *Xylt2*-deficient mice, conditional activation of AKT3 in osteoblasts will restore mTORC1 activity and rescue vertebral hypoplasia (confirmation); conversely, AKT3 knockout in these cells will exacerbate skeletal defects (refutation).

We hypothesize that TYMP (thymidine phosphorylase) deficiency leads to Spondyloepimetaphyseal dysplasia, Genevieve type, through impaired mitochondrial nucleotide homeostasis in chondrocytes, resulting in mtDNA instability and defective oxidative phosphorylation. Accumulation of thymidine due to reduced TYMP activity causes imbalanced mitochondrial dNTP pools, promoting mtDNA replication errors and depletion specifically in growth plate cartilage. This disrupts chondrocyte energy metabolism and differentiation, impairing endochondral ossification. We predict that patient-derived chondrocytes will exhibit elevated thymidine levels, mtDNA deletions, and reduced Complex I and IV activity—reversible upon thymidine depletion or recombinant TYMP supplementation. Conversely, normal mtDNA integrity and dNTP pools in these cells would refute the hypothesis. This mechanism aligns with TYMP’s role in nucleoside salvage and the disease’s skeletal-specific pathology, distinguishing it from systemic mitochondrial disorders.

We hypothesize that reduced activity of GTP cyclohydrolase 1 (GCH1), the rate-limiting enzyme in tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) biosynthesis, exacerbates mitochondrial dysfunction in Acyl-CoA dehydrogenase short-chain deficiency (SCADD) by impairing nitric oxide synthase (NOS) coupling. In SCADD, accumulation of short-chain acyl-CoAs (e.g., butyryl-CoA) may directly inhibit electron transfer in the mitochondrial β-oxidation pathway, and we propose that secondary BH4 deficiency due to GCH1 downregulation worsens this by increasing oxidative stress via uncoupled NOS-derived superoxide production. This would impair mitochondrial respiration and amplify metabolic insufficiency. Prediction: In fibroblasts from SCADD patients, pharmacologic enhancement of GCH1 activity (e.g., via sepiapterin supplementation) will restore BH4 levels, reduce protein nitrotyrosination, improve oxygen consumption rates, and decrease butyryl-CoA accumulation. Conversely, GCH1 inhibition will worsen these markers. Failure to improve mitochondrial function with BH4 rescue would refute this hypothesis.

We hypothesize that DOPA decarboxylase (DDC) exacerbates metabolic dysfunction in lethal neonatal carnitine palmitoyltransferase 2 (CPT2) deficiency by depleting cytosolic coenzyme A (CoA) through aberrant production of 3-methoxytyramine. In CPT2 deficiency, impaired mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation increases reliance on alternative energy substrates, elevating dopamine synthesis and DDC activity. We propose that sustained DDC-mediated dopamine decarboxylation consumes cysteamine, a CoA precursor, diverting it toward 3-methoxytyramine instead of CoA regeneration. This would further restrict already limited CoA availability, worsening the metabolic crisis. Prediction: In patient-derived fibroblasts with lethal neonatal CPT2 deficiency, pharmacological inhibition of DDC will increase free CoA levels and restore fatty acid oxidation flux (measured via \(^{14}\text{C}\)-palmitate oxidation to CO₂). Refutation: If DDC inhibition decreases CoA or fails to improve oxidation, the hypothesis is invalidated.

We hypothesize that BRCA1, a nuclear E3 ubiquitin ligase, regulates the stability of ASPM or other centrosomal proteins critical for mitotic fidelity during neurodevelopment, and that loss of BRCA1 function leads to aberrant ubiquitination, centrosome amplification, and defective neural progenitor cell division, contributing to the microcephaly and neuronal migration defects in Yunis-Varon syndrome (YVS). Although YVS is linked to *FIG4* mutations affecting phosphoinositide metabolism, we propose that BRCA1-mediated ubiquitination intersects with FIG4-regulated endosomal trafficking, and that disrupted BRCA1 activity exacerbates mitotic errors in neural precursors under conditions of FIG4 deficiency. Prediction: In *FIG4*-deficient human cerebral organoids, CRISPR-mediated *BRCA1* knockout will increase centrosome abnormalities and apoptosis (confirmatory), whereas BRCA1 overexpression will rescue mitotic defects (refutational if no rescue occurs).

We hypothesize that loss-of-function mutations in the glycine decarboxylase (GLDC) enzyme impair mitochondrial glycine cleavage system activity, leading to glycine accumulation and disruption of one-carbon metabolism, which compromises purine and thymidylate synthesis essential for rapidly developing skeletal and retinal tissues. Specifically, glycine-induced mitochondrial toxicity and reduced S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) availability impair proteoglycan methylation in growth plate cartilage and photoreceptor maintenance, contributing to spondylometaphyseal dysplasia and cone-rod dystrophy. We predict that patient-derived chondrocytes and retinal organoids will exhibit elevated glycine levels, reduced SAM, and defective sulfation of glycosaminoglycans. This hypothesis would be confirmed by rescue of methylation and differentiation defects upon glycine restriction or formate supplementation to restore one-carbon flux; failure of such interventions to correct phenotypes would refute the proposed mechanism.

We hypothesize that NDST1, a bifunctional enzyme with N-deacetylase and N-sulfotransferase activities involved in heparan sulfate biosynthesis, impairs mitochondrial nucleotide homeostasis via aberrant modification of mitochondrial outer membrane proteoglycans, contributing to Mitochondrial DNA depletion syndrome 21 (MTDPS21). Specifically, dysregulated NDST1 activity alters sulfation patterns on syndecan-4 or glypican-1, disrupting their interaction with nucleoside transporters or mitochondrial transcription factor A (TFAM), thereby reducing mitochondrial dNTP import or retention. We predict that knockdown of NDST1 in human fibroblasts will decrease mitochondrial heparan sulfate sulfation, correlate with reduced mtDNA copy number, and impair TFAM binding to mitochondrial nucleoids—results confirmed by qPCR and immunoprecipitation. Conversely, overexpression of wild-type NDST1, but not catalytically inactive NDST1 (S838A), will rescue mtDNA levels in NDST1-deficient cells. Failure to observe these effects would refute the hypothesis.

We hypothesize that PGAP4 deficiency disrupts glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI)-anchor remodeling, impairing the proper cell surface localization of specific GPI-anchored proteins essential for ocular development, thereby causing Microphthalmia, isolated, 8. Specifically, loss-of-function mutations in PGAP4 prevent the removal of an acyl chain from the GPI anchor in the Golgi, leading to increased shedding of GPI-anchored proteins (e.g., FGF receptors) from the plasma membrane via lipolytic cleavage. This mislocalization reduces FGF signaling in the developing optic vesicle, disrupting retinal progenitor proliferation. We predict that patient-derived iPSCs with PGAP4 mutations will show reduced surface levels of GPI-anchored proteins and diminished pERK activation in response to FGF2 during directed retinal differentiation, which would be rescued by wild-type PGAP4 expression. Conversely, normal surface protein expression and FGF signaling would refute this mechanism.

We hypothesize that loss-of-function mutations in IDH1 impair cytosolic NADPH production, leading to redox imbalance and defective myelin maintenance in corticospinal motor neurons, contributing to Spastic paraplegia 81, autosomal recessive. Reduced IDH1 activity decreases NADPH availability, compromising glutathione reductase-mediated recycling of reduced glutathione, thereby increasing vulnerability to oxidative stress in long axons. This mechanism specifically disrupts axonal integrity in upper motor neurons, consistent with the spastic paraplegia phenotype. We predict that patient-derived neurons with biallelic IDH1 mutations will exhibit decreased NADPH/NADP+ ratios, elevated reactive oxygen species, and axonal degeneration, all ameliorated by expression of wild-type IDH1 or treatment with cell-permeable NADPH precursors (e.g., nicotinamide riboside). Conversely, absence of these metabolic defects or failure of NADPH restoration to rescue the phenotype would refute the hypothesis. This proposal aligns with known IDH1 biochemistry and the autosomal recessive inheritance of SPG81.

We hypothesize that mitochondrial carbamoyl phosphate synthetase (CPS1), the rate-limiting enzyme of the urea cycle and a component of the MCAT complex in some contexts, promotes breast cancer progression by enhancing pyrimidine biosynthesis via increased carbamoyl phosphate availability. In triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), upregulated CPS1 diverts nitrogen from ammonia detoxification to de novo pyrimidine synthesis, supporting rapid proliferation. We predict that CPS1 knockdown in TNBC cell lines will reduce intracellular carbamoyl phosphate and orotic acid levels, impair DNA synthesis, and suppress tumor growth in xenograft models. Conversely, CPS1 overexpression will increase pyrimidine intermediates and accelerate proliferation. This hypothesis is falsifiable: if CPS1 knockdown fails to reduce pyrimidine pools or tumor growth despite adequate protein depletion, the proposed metabolic rewiring would be refuted. The link is grounded in CPS1’s dual role in nitrogen metabolism and nucleotide biosynthesis, specifically relevant to the high anabolic demands of aggressive breast cancers.

We hypothesize that DCXR (dicarbonyl and L-xylulose reductase) deficiency impairs the reduction of 3-oxo-Δ4 bile acid intermediates during bile acid synthesis, contributing to Congenital bile acid synthesis defect 2. Although AKR1D1 is the primary 5β-reductase in this pathway, DCXR—due to its structural similarity to aldo-keto reductases and ability to reduce α-dicarbonyl and ketone-containing substrates—may act as a secondary reductase for 3-oxo-Δ4 intermediates like 7α-hydroxy-4-cholesten-3-one. Loss-of-function mutations in DCXR could therefore reduce metabolic flux through the acidic bile acid synthesis pathway, leading to accumulation of hepatotoxic intermediate metabolites and reduced primary bile acid production, mirroring the phenotype of Congenital bile acid synthesis defect 2. This hypothesis predicts that DCXR-knockout human hepatocytes will exhibit reduced conversion of 7α-hydroxy-4-cholesten-3-one to 7α,12α-dihydroxy-5β-cholestan-3-one, detectable by LC-MS/MS. Restoration of conversion upon DCXR overexpression would confirm its role; no change would refute it.

We hypothesize that COLGALT2, which catalyzes the galactosylation of hydroxylysine residues in collagen, contributes to Dowling-Degos disease 4 through impaired post-translational modification of type XVII collagen (COL17A1), a structural component of epidermal hemidesmosomes. Mutations in *POGLUT1* cause Dowling-Degos disease 4, and since COLGALT2 functionally interacts with O-glucosylated proteins modified by POGLUT1, we propose that COLGALT2-mediated galactosylation is disrupted in *POGLUT1*-deficient keratinocytes, leading to defective collagen XVII maturation, compromised dermal-epidermal cohesion, and aberrant melanin transfer. We predict that siRNA knockdown of *COLGALT2* in human keratinocytes will reduce collagen XVII stability and recapitulate the hyperpigmentation and melanocyte dendricity seen in Dowling-Degos disease 4. Conversely, overexpression of *COLGALT2* in *POGLUT1*-mutant keratinocytes will partially rescue collagen XVII levels and normalize pigmentation in co-culture with melanocytes. Failure to observe these effects would refute the hypothesis.

We hypothesize that BCL2 impairs mitochondrial calcium uptake by disrupting the interaction between the inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate receptor (IP3R) and the mitochondrial calcium uniporter (MCU) complex, leading to reduced stimulation of tricarboxylic acid (TAC) cycle dehydrogenases and subsequent diminished electron transport chain (ETC) activity in Combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency 57 (COXPD57). This disease, caused by mutations in mitochondrial aspartyl-tRNA synthetase (DARS2), already compromises mitochondrial translation and ETC complex assembly; we propose that BCL2 overexpression exacerbates bioenergetic failure by sequestering IP3R at the endoplasmic reticulum, thereby limiting calcium-dependent activation of mitochondrial metabolism. Prediction: In DARS2-deficient cells, BCL2 overexpression will reduce mitochondrial calcium transients and NADH production, worsening oxidative phosphorylation (confirmed by decreased oxygen consumption rates). Conversely, BCL2 inhibition or IP3R-MCU disruption will rescue calcium flux and NADH levels, refuting the hypothesis if no improvement occurs.

We hypothesize that loss-of-function mutations in ABCB11 impair canalicular bile acid export, leading to intracellular bile acid accumulation that disrupts endoplasmic reticulum (ER) homeostasis and induces ER stress in developing neural and epidermal tissues. This stress exacerbates impaired serine biosynthesis—already compromised in Neu-Laxova syndrome 2 due to PHGDH mutations—by reducing the availability of ER-dependent enzymes in the phosphorylated serine pathway. Consequently, severe serine deficiency disrupts neural tube closure and skin development, amplifying the syndrome’s hallmark malformations. We predict that patient-derived hepatocytes or neural progenitor cells with ABCB11 mutations will show elevated ER stress markers (e.g., CHOP, BiP) and reduced phosphoserine levels compared to controls. This hypothesis would be confirmed by these findings and rescued serine synthesis upon chemical chaperone (e.g., 4-PBA) treatment; it would be refuted if ABCB11 deficiency shows no impact on ER stress or serine metabolites in PHGDH-deficient cellular models.

We hypothesize that TRI-TAT2-2 (tryptophan 2,3-dioxygenase 2 isoform 2) exacerbates oxidative stress in Prolidase deficiency by increasing kynurenine pathway flux, leading to accumulation of redox-active metabolites that impair residual prolidase activity. In Prolidase deficiency, impaired degradation of iminodipeptides already disrupts collagen turnover and increases cellular stress; we propose that upregulated TRI-TAT2-2 further shifts tryptophan metabolism toward quinolinic acid, generating reactive oxygen species that oxidize the manganese-containing active site of prolidase. We predict that fibroblasts from Prolidase-deficient patients with elevated TRI-TAT2-2 expression will show reduced prolidase activity and increased protein carbonylation, reversible by kynurenine pathway inhibition (e.g., with 680C91). Conversely, genetic knockdown of TRI-TAT2-2 should restore prolidase function and decrease oxidative damage markers. Refutation would occur if TRI-TAT2-2 modulation shows no effect on prolidase activity or oxidative stress markers in this context.

We hypothesize that ELOVL5 deficiency disrupts the synthesis of very long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids (VLC-PUFAs), impairing neuronal membrane integrity and synaptic function in developing pontocerebellar neurons, thereby contributing to the neurodevelopmental pathology of Pontocerebellar hypoplasia 2D (PCH2D). Specifically, loss-of-function mutations in *TSEN54*, the primary genetic cause of PCH2D, may downregulate ELOVL5 expression or activity, reducing C28–C36 PUFA levels critical for cerebellar neurogenesis and axonal guidance. We predict that fibroblasts or induced neural progenitor cells from PCH2D patients with *TSEN54* mutations will show significantly reduced ELOVL5 mRNA and protein levels, accompanied by decreased VLC-PUFA abundance. This would be confirmed by lipidomic analysis showing >50% reduction in C32:6n-3 and C36:6n-3 species, and refuted if VLC-PUFA levels remain unchanged despite *TSEN54* mutation.

We hypothesize that ATP6V1FP2, a subunit of the vacuolar H⁺-ATPase (V-ATPase) complex, impairs endolysosomal acidification, disrupting intracellular trafficking of COQ proteins required for Coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10) biosynthesis, thereby contributing to Coenzyme Q10 deficiency, primary, 1. Specifically, loss-of-function mutations in ATP6V1FP2 may compromise V-ATPase assembly, leading to defective endosomal maturation and mislocalization of COQ3, COQ4, or COQ7 to non-functional compartments. This would reduce CoQ10 biosynthesis despite intact COQ genes. We predict that fibroblasts from patients with ATP6V1FP2 mutations will show elevated lysosomal pH, aberrant COQ protein localization, and reduced CoQ10 levels; these defects should be rescued by wild-type ATP6V1FP2 expression. Conversely, absence of these phenotypes or no CoQ10 restoration upon ATP6V1FP2 complementation would refute the hypothesis. This mechanism directly links V-ATPase dysfunction to primary CoQ10 deficiency via disrupted organelle acidification and protein trafficking.

terminal_shown: Epileptic encephalopathy, infantile or early childhood, 3
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that BAD (Bcl-2-associated death promoter) dysfunction disrupts mitochondrial metabolism in developing neurons by impairing glucose utilization and ATP generation, contributing to Epileptic encephalopathy, infantile or early childhood, 3 (EIEE3). Specifically, BAD regulates glucokinase activity and mitochondrial hexokinase binding, coupling metabolic flux to cell survival. Loss-of-function mutations in BAD may reduce neuronal bioenergetic capacity during critical developmental windows, increasing seizure susceptibility and encephalopathy. We predict that Bad-knockout mice expressing Scn1a haploinsufficiency (a model of EIEE3) will exhibit earlier seizure onset and reduced hippocampal ATP levels compared to Scn1a mutants alone. Conversely, neuronal-specific expression of phospho-mimetic BAD (S155E) should restore metabolic flexibility and delay seizures. Refutation would occur if BAD deletion shows no effect on seizure severity or brain energy metabolism in EIEE3 models, or if BAD’s metabolic targets remain unchanged in affected neurons.

We hypothesize that NDUFA10 deficiency impairs mitochondrial complex I function in adrenal zona fasciculata cells, reducing ATP production required for CYP11B1-mediated 11β-hydroxylation of 11-deoxycortisol to cortisol, thereby causing Glucocorticoid deficiency 5. Specifically, diminished NDUFA10 activity decreases NAD⁺/NADH cycling, lowering the proton motive force and ATP synthesis, which compromises steroidogenic electron transfer via adrenodoxin reductase and adrenodoxin. This disrupts cortisol biosynthesis without affecting mineralocorticoid pathways, consistent with isolated glucocorticoid deficiency. We predict that adrenal-specific *Ndufa10* knockout mice will exhibit reduced cortisol (but normal aldosterone), elevated plasma ACTH, and adrenal lipid accumulation. These effects would be rescued by targeted expression of wild-type NDUFA10, but not by catalytically dead mutants. Conversely, normal cortisol levels in these knockouts would refute the hypothesis.

terminal_shown: Skeletal dysplasia, mild, with joint laxity and advanced bone age
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that impaired activity of 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase-like protein (HAAO) leads to mild skeletal dysplasia with joint laxity and advanced bone age due to disrupted catabolism of tryptophan and subsequent accumulation of bioactive metabolites that interfere with collagen cross-linking and growth plate regulation. HAAO catalyzes the conversion of 3-hydroxyanthranilic acid to quinolinic acid in the kynurenine pathway. We propose that HAAO deficiency causes 3-hydroxyanthranilic acid accumulation, which aberrantly inhibits lysyl hydroxylase (PLOD2), an enzyme critical for collagen fibril stability in connective tissues. This would reduce hydroxylysine-mediated cross-links in type I collagen, impairing bone and joint integrity. Prediction: In HAAO-knockdown chondrocytes, we will observe decreased collagen cross-linking (measured by mass spectrometry) and accelerated mineralization (via Alizarin Red staining); these effects will be rescued by 3-hydroxyanthranilic acid scavenging. Failure to observe these changes would refute the hypothesis.

We hypothesize that NDUFA5, a subunit of mitochondrial complex I, indirectly influences the stability or activity of molybdenum cofactor (Moco) sulfurase, the enzyme deficient in Xanthinuria 2 due to mutations in *MOCOS*. Impaired NDUFA5 function disrupts mitochondrial redox balance, increasing reactive oxygen species (ROS) that oxidize the Moco, rendering it unusable by xanthine dehydrogenase (XDH). This would phenocopy MOCOS deficiency, reducing uric acid production and increasing xanthine accumulation. We predict that *NDUFA5*-knockdown human hepatocytes will show decreased XDH activity and elevated xanthine levels—phenotypes rescued by antioxidant treatment (e.g., N-acetylcysteine). Conversely, if XDH activity remains normal despite *NDUFA5* loss, or if antioxidants fail to restore it, the hypothesis is refuted. This mechanism specifically links NDUFA5-mediated redox imbalance to the biochemical hallmark of Xanthinuria 2: xanthine overproduction due to functional XDH deficiency.

We hypothesize that dysfunction of the NDUFS1 subunit of mitochondrial Complex I exacerbates oxidative stress in Molybdenum cofactor deficiency C (MoCD-C) by impairing NADH-driven electron transport, thereby increasing superoxide production when sulfite oxidase is inactive. In MoCD-C, loss of functional MOCS3 disrupts molybdenum cofactor synthesis, inactivating sulfite oxidase and causing sulfite accumulation. We propose that accumulated sulfite directly inhibits NDUFS1, further compromising Complex I and creating a feedforward loop of mitochondrial ROS generation. This synergy would amplify neuronal oxidative damage, accelerating neurodegeneration. Prediction: In MoCD-C patient-derived neurons, NDUFS1 activity will be reduced compared to controls, and sulfite exposure will dose-dependently inhibit recombinant NDUFS1-containing Complex I in vitro. Refutation: If NDUFS1 activity remains unaffected by sulfite in purified systems or if ROS levels decrease despite combined MoCD-C and NDUFS1 deficiency, the proposed mechanism is invalidated.

We hypothesize that FASLG (Fas ligand) exacerbates mitochondrial dysfunction in Phosphohydroxylysinuria by promoting Fas-mediated apoptosis in metabolically stressed cells. In this rare inborn error of lysine metabolism, accumulation of phosphohydroxylysine may impair mitochondrial respiration, increasing reactive oxygen species and sensitizing cells—particularly hepatocytes and neurons—to extrinsic apoptosis. FASLG, by engaging Fas receptors, could amplify caspase-8 activation and cross-talk with the intrinsic apoptotic pathway via BID cleavage, accelerating cell death in tissues already compromised by metabolic stress. We predict that FASLG knockout or inhibition in a cellular model of Phosphohydroxylysinuria (e.g., patient-derived fibroblasts) will reduce caspase-3/7 activation and improve cell viability under lysine loading, confirming the hypothesis. Conversely, exogenous FASLG stimulation should worsen apoptosis in these cells but not in wild-type controls, refuting the hypothesis if no difference is observed. This mechanism links immune-mediated apoptosis to metabolic vulnerability in Phosphohydroxylysinuria.

We hypothesize that ELOVL5, which catalyzes elongation of C18 and C20 polyunsaturated fatty acids, exacerbates metabolic dysfunction in infantile carnitine palmitoyltransferase 2 (CPT2) deficiency by increasing the cellular burden of long-chain fatty acid (LCFA) substrates that cannot be efficiently transported into mitochondria for β-oxidation. In CPT2 deficiency, impaired translocation of LCFA-carnitine esters limits energy production and promotes toxic accumulation of long-chain acyl-CoAs. Elevated ELOVL5 activity would amplify this pathology by increasing the synthesis of very-long-chain fatty acids (e.g., C20:4, C22:6), further saturating the compromised CPT2-dependent import pathway. We predict that genetic or pharmacological inhibition of ELOVL5 in CPT2-deficient infantile hepatocytes will reduce intracellular accumulation of long- and very-long-chain acyl-CoAs and improve β-oxidation flux. Conversely, ELOVL5 overexpression will worsen metabolite accumulation and energy deficit. These outcomes would confirm or refute ELOVL5’s role in modulating substrate overload in this specific disease.

We hypothesize that DLL3 (Delta-like protein 3) disrupts hepatic iron homeostasis by aberrantly activating Notch signaling in hepatocytes, leading to suppression of hepcidin (HAMP) expression, increased iron accumulation, and consequent iron-mediated oxidative activation of uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase (UROD) inhibition in Familial porphyria cutanea tarda (F-PCT). In F-PCT, inherited UROD deficiency predisposes individuals to enzyme inactivation under oxidative stress; excess iron catalyzes reactive oxygen species that further impair residual UROD activity. We predict that DLL3 overexpression in hepatocyte-specific mouse models will decrease HAMP expression, increase liver iron, elevate urinary uroporphyrin levels, and exacerbate photosensitivity—effects reversible with Notch pathway inhibition. Conversely, DLL3 knockout in a Urod-deficient background will restore hepcidin, reduce iron overload, and normalize porphyrin accumulation. These outcomes would confirm the hypothesis; absence of iron or porphyrin changes despite DLL3 modulation would refute it.

We hypothesize that ABCC2 dysfunction impairs peroxisomal export of toxic bile acid intermediates, exacerbating metabolic stress in Rhizomelic chondrodysplasia punctata 2 (RCDP2), which arises from PEX7 mutations and defective peroxisomal matrix protein import. In RCDP2, compromised peroxisomal function may lead to accumulation of phytanic acid and atypical bile acid precursors. ABCC2, localized to the peroxisomal membrane in hepatocytes, likely mediates efflux of these metabolites. Impaired ABCC2 activity would increase intraperoxisomal concentrations of cytotoxic compounds, worsening oxidative damage and further disrupting plasmalogen biosynthesis—a key defect in RCDP2. We predict that ABCC2 knockdown in PEX7-deficient fibroblasts will reduce plasmalogen synthesis by ≥50% compared to controls (confirming the hypothesis), whereas overexpression of functional ABCC2 will restore plasmalogen levels by ≥30% (refuting it). This interaction is testable via stable isotope labeling and lipidomics in genetically modified RCDP2 cell models.

We hypothesize that NDUFA5, a subunit of mitochondrial complex I, impairs adrenal steroidogenesis in Glucocorticoid deficiency 5 by disrupting NAD⁺/NADH redox balance, thereby reducing the availability of NADPH required for cytochrome P450 11B1 (CYP11B1) activity in the zona fasciculata. Specifically, defective NDUFA5 compromises electron transport chain efficiency, leading to elevated mitochondrial NADH levels and diminished NADPH regeneration via nicotinamide nucleotide transhydrogenase (NNT), ultimately limiting cortisol synthesis. We predict that adrenal cells with biallelic NDUFA5 mutations will exhibit reduced CYP11B1-dependent cortisol production, which can be rescued by exogenous NADPH or NNT overexpression. Conversely, this defect will not be rescued by cAMP stimulation of steroidogenic acute regulatory protein (StAR). This hypothesis is falsified if NDUFA5-deficient cells show normal cortisol output despite intact StAR and CYP11B1 expression, or if NADPH supplementation fails to restore cortisol synthesis.

We hypothesize that TRT-AGT1-3, a putative heme-responsive serine/threonine kinase, exacerbates acute intermittent porphyria (AIP) by phosphorylating and inhibiting hydroxymethylbilane synthase (HMBS), the enzyme deficient in AIP. Under conditions of heme depletion, elevated TRT-AGT1-3 activity reduces residual HMBS function, amplifying accumulation of neurotoxic porphyrin precursors (ALA and PBG). Specifically, we predict that in hepatocytes derived from AIP model mice, CRISPR-mediated knockout of TRT-AGT1-3 will increase HMBS activity by ≥40% and reduce PBG levels by ≥50% during chemical induction of porphyria (e.g., phenobarbital challenge), as measured by enzymatic assay and HPLC. Conversely, overexpression of wild-type TRT-AGT1-3—but not a kinase-dead mutant (K42A)—will decrease HMBS activity and elevate PBG. Refutation would occur if TRT-AGT1-3 knockout fails to restore HMBS activity or reduce PBG under these conditions, or if no direct phosphorylation of HMBS by TRT-AGT1-3 is detectable via immunoprecipitation-kinase assay.

We hypothesize that COX10 deficiency impairs cytochrome c oxidase (COX) assembly in lens mitochondria, leading to defective oxidative phosphorylation, chronic oxidative stress, and aggregation of crystallin proteins in lens fiber cells, thereby promoting cataract formation in Cataract 44. Specifically, reduced COX10-mediated heme a biosynthesis diminishes COX activity, increasing mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS) that overwhelm antioxidant defenses (e.g., glutathione) in the avascular lens. This oxidative damage disrupts lens transparency by modifying crystallins and promoting insoluble protein aggregates. We predict that lens-specific *COX10* knockout mice will exhibit elevated lens ROS, reduced COX activity, crystallin aggregation, and cataract development resembling human Cataract 44. Conversely, preservation of COX activity and absence of cataracts in *COX10*-deficient mice supplemented with mitochondrial-targeted antioxidants (e.g., MitoQ) would refute a primary role of oxidative stress in this mechanism.

terminal_shown: Congenital hemidysplasia with ichthyosiform erythroderma and limb defects
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that pathogenic variants in the mitochondrial valyl-tRNA synthetase VARS2 impair mitochondrial protein translation, leading to defective oxidative phosphorylation and increased reactive oxygen species (ROS) in embryonic ectodermal and mesodermal tissues. This bioenergetic deficit disrupts Wnt and SHH signaling pathways critical for limb patterning and epidermal differentiation, contributing to the asymmetric limb defects and ichthyosiform erythroderma characteristic of Congenital Hemidysplasia with Ichthyosiform Erythroderma and Limb Defects (CHILD syndrome). Specifically, we predict that patient-derived fibroblasts with biallelic VARS2 mutations will exhibit reduced oxygen consumption rates, diminished levels of mt-tRNAVal charging, and aberrant activation of Wnt/β-catenin signaling under differentiation conditions. These phenotypes would be rescued by wild-type VARS2 expression. Conversely, absence of these defects in patient cells or failure of VARS2 re-expression to restore mitochondrial function and signaling would refute the hypothesis.

We hypothesize that loss-of-function mutations in EPRS1 impair its canonical role in charging glutamyl-prolyl-tRNA during protein synthesis, leading to defective collagen prolyl hydroxylation due to reduced proline availability in the endoplasmic reticulum. In Rhizomelic dysplasia, Ain-Naz type—characterized by severe skeletal shortening and defective endochondral ossification—this shortage would specifically disrupt the folding and stability of type II collagen, a proline-rich extracellular matrix protein essential for cartilage integrity. We predict that patient-derived chondrocytes with EPRS1 mutations will exhibit decreased intracellular proline levels, elevated unfolded protein response markers, and intracellular retention of type II collagen. This hypothesis would be confirmed by rescuing collagen secretion and chondrocyte viability upon proline supplementation or EPRS1 re-expression, and refuted if proline supplementation fails to correct collagen trafficking defects despite restored EPRS1 activity.

We hypothesize that PNPO (pyridoxine 5′-phosphate oxidase) deficiency disrupts cellular pyridoxal 5′-phosphate (PLP) homeostasis, leading to aberrant post-translational modification of proteins involved in skeletal development, thereby exacerbating the hyperostosis and craniofacial dysplasia in Lenz-Majewski hyperostotic dwarfism (LMS). Specifically, reduced PNPO activity decreases PLP availability, impairing lysyl oxidase (LOX) function—an enzyme requiring PLP as a cofactor for cross-linking collagen and elastin. Dysregulated extracellular matrix maturation may amplify the pathological bone overgrowth driven by mutant PTDSS1. We predict that fibroblasts from LMS patients with concomitant PNPO inhibition will show reduced LOX activity, disorganized collagen fibrils, and increased mineralization *in vitro*—a phenotype rescued by PLP supplementation. Conversely, normal mineralization with PLP treatment would refute a significant role for PNPO-PLP-LOX disruption in LMS pathology.

We hypothesize that loss-of-function mutations in the choline kinase alpha (CHKA) enzyme impair phosphatidylcholine biosynthesis, leading to disrupted neuronal membrane integrity and aberrant synaptic vesicle trafficking in Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy 36 (DEE36). Reduced CHKA activity decreases phosphocholine production, limiting the Kennedy pathway flux and compromising membrane phospholipid homeostasis in developing neurons. This deficit promotes hyperexcitability and defective neurotransmission, contributing to early-onset seizures and neurodevelopmental delay characteristic of DEE36. We predict that patient-derived neurons with biallelic CHKA mutations will exhibit decreased phosphatidylcholine levels and abnormal synaptic vesicle recycling, measurable via mass spectrometry and FM dye imaging. These phenotypes should be rescued by reintroduction of wild-type CHKA, but not by catalytically inactive CHKA (G222R). Failure to observe phospholipid deficits or synaptic dysfunction in mutant neurons would refute this hypothesis.

We hypothesize that DHRSX deficiency impairs NADPH-dependent reduction of lipid peroxidation-derived aldehydes in megakaryocytes, leading to oxidative stress-induced apoptosis and defective platelet production in Thrombocytopenia 13, syndromic. DHRSX, a retinal reductase with NADPH-dependent activity, may protect hematopoietic cells by detoxifying cytotoxic aldehydes such as 4-hydroxynonenal. In loss-of-function states, accumulated aldehydes disrupt mitochondrial integrity, activating caspase-9 and impairing proplatelet formation. We predict that DHRSX-knockdown human megakaryocytes will exhibit elevated 4-HNE adducts, increased apoptosis, and reduced platelet shedding—phenotypes rescued by exogenous NADPH or aldehyde scavengers like hydralazine. Conversely, overexpression of wild-type DHRSX, but not a catalytically inactive mutant (S166A), will restore redox balance and normal thrombopoiesis. These outcomes would confirm a direct protective role for DHRSX in megakaryocyte maturation; lack of rescue by enzymatically inactive DHRSX or no change in aldehyde load would refute the hypothesis.

We hypothesize that NT5C1B-RDH14, a bifunctional enzyme with 5'-nucleotidase and retinol dehydrogenase activities, impairs dolichol recycling in Congenital Disorder of Glycosylation 1J (CDG-IJ) by reducing the availability of dolichol phosphate, a critical lipid carrier for N-glycosylation. Specifically, its retinol dehydrogenase activity may deplete cellular retinol pools required for dolichol regeneration via the mevalonate pathway. We predict that knockdown of NT5C1B-RDH14 in CDG-IJ patient fibroblasts will restore dolichol phosphate levels and improve N-glycosylation efficiency, evidenced by normalized transferrin isoform profiles. Conversely, overexpression of NT5C1B-RDH14 in wild-type cells will reduce dolichol phosphate and recapitulate the hypoglycosylation phenotype. This hypothesis is falsifiable: if NT5C1B-RDH14 modulation fails to alter dolichol metabolism or N-glycosylation status, the proposed mechanistic link is invalidated.

We hypothesize that FPGT (fucose-1-phosphate guanylyltransferase) contributes to Barrett esophagus by aberrantly modifying O-glycans in esophageal epithelial cells during chronic acid reflux, leading to disrupted mucosal integrity and metaplastic transformation. Specifically, elevated FPGT activity increases GDP-L-fucose production, driving fucosylation of cell surface glycoproteins such as MUC1 and CDH1 (E-cadherin), which alters cell adhesion and promotes a columnar, intestinal-like phenotype characteristic of Barrett esophagus. We predict that FPGT overexpression in esophageal squamous epithelial cells exposed to acidic bile salts will increase core fucosylation, accelerate metaplastic changes in vitro, and disrupt tight junctions. This hypothesis would be confirmed by detecting elevated FPGT expression and fucosylated glycoforms in Barrett esophagus tissues versus normal controls via immunohistochemistry and mass spectrometry, and refuted if FPGT knockdown fails to reduce fucosylation and metaplastic differentiation under acidic conditions.

We hypothesize that CH25H (cholesterol 25-hydroxylase) exacerbates neuroinflammation in adenylosuccinase deficiency by amplifying microglial activation through 25-hydroxycholesterol (25-OHC)-mediated disruption of purine metabolism. In adenylosuccinase deficiency, accumulation of succinylaminoimidazole carboxamide ribose (SAICAr) and succinyladenosine (S-Ado) impairs de novo purine synthesis and signaling. We propose that CH25H-derived 25-OHC, an oxysterol that modulates membrane fluidity and LXR signaling, further inhibits residual adenylosuccinase activity or disrupts purinosome assembly by altering cholesterol-rich microdomains. This synergy worsens purine depletion and toxic metabolite accumulation. Prediction: In patient-derived neurons and glia, CH25H inhibition or knockout will reduce SAICAr/S-Ado levels and IL-1β release, improving ATP synthesis (confirmation); conversely, CH25H overexpression will elevate SAICAr and neuroinflammatory markers despite unchanged adenylosuccinase expression (refutation).

We hypothesize that GUSB (beta-glucuronidase) deficiency indirectly disrupts mitochondrial proline catabolism by impairing lysosomal degradation of glycosaminoglycans, leading to secondary accumulation of toxic metabolites that inhibit proline dehydrogenase (PRODH), the enzyme deficient in Hyperprolinemia 2. Specifically, undegraded heparan sulfate may leak into the cytosol and bind to PRODH in the mitochondrial membrane, reducing its activity and causing proline accumulation. We predict that fibroblasts from GUSB-deficient individuals will exhibit elevated intracellular proline levels and reduced PRODH activity compared to controls; this effect will be reversed upon exogenous addition of recombinant GUSB or heparan sulfate-degrading enzymes. Conversely, no significant change in proline metabolism is expected if GUSB loss does not alter PRODH function. This hypothesis links lysosomal dysfunction directly to impaired proline catabolism, offering a novel mechanism contributing to the Hyperprolinemia 2 biochemical phenotype.

We hypothesize that ELOVL6, which catalyzes elongation of C12–C16 saturated and monounsaturated fatty acids, contributes to Cole disease pathogenesis by altering the acyl chain composition of glycosphingolipids in melanosomes. Dysregulated ELOVL6 activity may lead to aberrant C16:0 to C18:0 fatty acid ratios in ceramides, disrupting membrane microdomain organization and impairing melanosome maturation or tyrosinase trafficking in melanocytes. This defect would manifest as the hypopigmented macules with hyperkeratotic borders characteristic of Cole disease. We predict that ELOVL6 knockdown in human melanocyte cultures will normalize glycosphingolipid saturation profiles and restore melanosomal morphology and pigmentation, confirming the hypothesis. Conversely, if pigmentation defects persist despite ELOVL6 suppression or if ELOVL6 expression levels show no correlation with C18:0-ceramide accumulation in Cole disease patient biopsies, the hypothesis is refuted. This mechanism is distinct from known WNT or EDAR pathways implicated in other pigmentation disorders.

terminal_shown: Muscular dystrophy, congenital hearing loss, and ovarian insufficiency syndrome
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that CDO1 (cysteine dioxygenase type 1) deficiency impairs taurine biosynthesis, leading to reduced taurine levels that disrupt mitochondrial function and antioxidant defense in metabolically active tissues, thereby contributing to the pathogenesis of muscular dystrophy, congenital hearing loss, and ovarian insufficiency syndrome. Specifically, diminished CDO1 activity decreases hypotaurine and taurine production, compromising taurine-conjugated mitochondrial tRNAs and increasing oxidative stress in skeletal muscle, cochlear hair cells, and ovarian granulosa cells. We predict that CDO1-knockout mice will exhibit reduced taurine levels, mitochondrial dysfunction, and histopathological features of all three disorders—muscle degeneration, cochlear apoptosis, and follicular depletion—reversed by dietary taurine supplementation. Conversely, absence of these phenotypes in CDO1-knockout mice or failure of taurine supplementation to ameliorate symptoms would refute the hypothesis. This mechanism is grounded in taurine’s established roles in membrane stabilization, ROS scavenging, and mitochondrial translation fidelity.

terminal_shown: Leber-like hereditary optic neuropathy, autosomal recessive 2
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that mutations in COX10 impair heme a biosynthesis, disrupting assembly of mitochondrial complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase) in retinal ganglion cells, thereby reducing oxidative phosphorylation efficiency and increasing reactive oxygen species (ROS) in the optic nerve. This bioenergetic deficit preferentially damages the metabolically active papillomacular bundle, leading to the degeneration observed in Leber-like hereditary optic neuropathy, autosomal recessive 2. Specifically, we predict that patient-derived optic nerve astrocytes with biallelic COX10 mutations will exhibit decreased complex IV activity, reduced heme a levels, and elevated ROS—rescuable by lentiviral-mediated expression of wild-type COX10. Conversely, absence of these defects in patient cells or failure of wild-type COX10 to restore complex IV function and reduce ROS would refute the hypothesis. These experiments will test a direct mechanistic link between COX10 dysfunction and the pathophysiology of this specific optic neuropathy.

We hypothesize that RDH12, a retinol dehydrogenase localized in the endoplasmic reticulum, impairs N-linked glycosylation in Congenital Disorder of Glycosylation 1L (CDG1L) by disrupting the dolichol cycle through aberrant metabolism of lipid-linked precursors. Specifically, RDH12 may oxidize dolichol or its phosphorylated intermediates, reducing the pool of dolichol-phosphate required for assembly of the lipid-linked oligosaccharide (LLO) precursor Glc₃Man₉GlcNAc₂-PP-dolichol. This would lead to underglycosylation of target proteins, consistent with CDG1L pathology. We predict that RDH12 overexpression in CDG1L patient fibroblasts will reduce LLO levels and worsen hypoglycosylation, while RDH12 knockdown or inhibition will restore LLO synthesis and improve glycosylation. Conversely, loss of this effect in cells lacking functional RDH12 or supplemented with exogenous dolichol-phosphate would refute the hypothesis. This mechanism links RDH12’s substrate promiscuity to a direct role in dolichol metabolism, exacerbating the ALG12 deficiency characteristic of CDG1L.

We hypothesize that B3GALT4 deficiency disrupts the biosynthesis of specific glycosphingolipids in neural crest-derived periocular mesenchyme, impairing cell surface glycosylation essential for PAX6 signaling and corneal endothelial migration during anterior eye development, thereby contributing to Anterior segment dysgenesis 6 (ASGD6). Specifically, loss of B3GALT4-mediated β-1,3-galactosylation of glycosphingolipid precursors alters lipid raft composition and PAX6 receptor localization or stability. We predict that B3galt4-knockout mice will exhibit anterior segment malformations (e.g., iridocorneal angle defects, corneal opacity) and reduced PAX6 expression in periocular tissues—phenocopying ASGD6. This hypothesis would be confirmed by immunohistochemical detection of disrupted PAX6 localization and reduced GM1/Lc3 glycosphingolipids in B3galt4-deficient embryonic eyes, and refuted if glycosphingolipid profiles and PAX6 expression remain normal despite B3galt4 loss.

terminal_shown: Spondyloepimetaphyseal dysplasia with joint laxity, 1, with or without fractures
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that mutations in the HTD2 enzyme, which catalyzes the hydroxylation of lysine residues in collagen precursors within the endoplasmic reticulum, impair the post-translational modification of type II collagen (COL2A1). This defect reduces collagen cross-linking in cartilage extracellular matrix, compromising structural integrity in growth plates and articular cartilage. In spondyloepimetaphyseal dysplasia with joint laxity, 1 (SEMD-JL1), such matrix instability would manifest as skeletal dysplasia, joint hypermobility, and fracture susceptibility. We predict that fibroblasts from SEMD-JL1 patients with HTD2 mutations will exhibit reduced lysyl hydroxylation in COL2A1, detectable by mass spectrometry, and abnormal collagen fibril ultrastructure on electron microscopy. This hypothesis would be confirmed by these findings and refuted if hydroxylation levels and fibril morphology are normal despite HTD2 mutations, or if HTD2 loss does not impair COL2A1 secretion or stability in chondrocyte models.

We hypothesize that RIMKLB, through aberrant phosphorylation of the mitochondrial bile acid biosynthesis enzyme 3β-hydroxy-Δ5-C27-steroid oxidoreductase (HSD3B7), impairs its stability or catalytic activity, contributing to Congenital bile acid synthesis defect 1 (CBAS1). Although HSD3B7 mutations are the primary cause of CBAS1, we propose that RIMKLB-mediated post-translational modification disrupts HSD3B7 function even in individuals without HSD3B7 mutations, phenocopying the disease. Specifically, we predict that overexpression of RIMKLB in hepatocyte cell lines will decrease HSD3B7 activity and lead to accumulation of Δ5-3β-hydroxy bile acid intermediates—measurable via LC-MS/MS. Conversely, CRISPR-mediated knockout of RIMKLB should restore normal bile acid profiles in these cells. Detection of RIMKLB-HSD3B7 co-immunoprecipitation and in vitro phosphorylation of HSD3B7 by RIMKLB would confirm direct interaction. Failure to observe phosphorylation or metabolic changes despite RIMKLB modulation would refute this hypothesis.

We hypothesize that loss-of-function mutations in *ACAT1* (acetyl-CoA acetyltransferase 1) disrupt mitochondrial ketone body metabolism in oligodendrocytes, impairing myelin lipid synthesis and contributing to hypomyelination in Leukodystrophy, hypomyelinating, 9. ACAT1 catalyzes the condensation of two acetyl-CoA molecules to form acetoacetyl-CoA, a critical step in ketone body utilization. Oligodendrocytes rely on ketone bodies as an alternative energy and carbon source during active myelination. Impaired ACAT1 function would reduce acetoacetyl-CoA availability, limiting cytoplasmic acetyl-CoA pools required for fatty acid and cholesterol synthesis—key components of myelin. We predict that *ACAT1*-deficient patient-derived oligodendrocytes will exhibit reduced myelin basic protein expression and defective myelination in co-culture with neurons, which can be rescued by supplementation with ketone bodies (e.g., β-hydroxybutyrate) or acetoacetate, but not glucose. Failure to rescue myelination with ketone bodies would refute this mechanism.

We hypothesize that GPHN (gephyrin), a molybdenum cofactor (Moco) biosynthesis enzyme, impairs early N-glycosylation in Congenital Disorder of Glycosylation 2D (CDG-II D) due to disrupted dolichol-phosphate-mannose (Dol-P-Man) synthesis secondary to Moco deficiency. Specifically, GPHN’s role in Moco-dependent sulfite oxidase activity influences cellular redox balance; GPHN dysfunction leads to sulfite accumulation and oxidative stress, which inactivates DPM1, the catalytic subunit of Dol-P-Man synthase. This disrupts protein mannosylation in the ER, a hallmark of CDG-II D. We predict that patient-derived cells with GPHN mutations will show reduced DPM1 activity, aberrant transferrin glycosylation, and elevated sulfite levels—reversed by antioxidant treatment or functional Moco supplementation. Conversely, normal glycosylation in GPHN-deficient cells under low-oxidative conditions would refute this mechanism. This hypothesis links GPHN’s canonical Moco role to CDG-II D via redox-sensitive glycosylation machinery, offering a novel, testable pathway distinct from primary glycosyltransferase defects.

We hypothesize that PCYOX1 deficiency impairs mitochondrial coenzyme Q (CoQ) redox cycling by disrupting the degradation of prenylcysteine intermediates, leading to aberrant accumulation of farnesylcysteine in the inner mitochondrial membrane. This accumulation competitively inhibits CoQ-dependent electron transfer in respiratory complexes I/II and III, specifically reducing electron flux through the mitochondrial respiratory chain. Because Combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency 20 (COXPD20) is linked to defective assembly or function of oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) complexes I, III, and IV, we propose that chronic PCYOX1 loss disrupts CoQ-mediated electron shuttling, secondarily impairing OXPHOS supercomplex stability. Prediction: In PCYOX1-knockdown cells, we will observe decreased oxygen consumption rates (OCR), particularly under conditions demanding electron transport chain flux, and increased farnesylcysteine levels; these defects will be rescued by exogenous CoQ10 supplementation. Failure to rescue OCR with CoQ10 would refute this mechanism.

We hypothesize that deficient inosine triphosphate pyrophosphatase (ITPA) activity leads to toxic accumulation of inosine triphosphate (ITP) in fetal motor neurons, causing aberrant purine metabolism and impaired ATP-dependent chaperone function during neuromuscular development, thereby contributing to the pathogenesis of lethal congenital contracture syndrome 2 (LCCS2). Specifically, elevated ITP competes with ATP for binding to HSP90 and other ATP-dependent folding proteins, disrupting the proper folding of critical neuronal and neuromuscular junction proteins such as GLE1, the protein deficient in LCCS2. We predict that ITPA-knockdown in a human embryonic stem cell-derived motor neuron model of LCCS2 will exacerbate protein misfolding, reduce GLE1 stability, and increase apoptosis. Conversely, overexpression of functional ITPA will restore GLE1 levels and improve neuronal survival. These outcomes would confirm the hypothesis; lack of effect would refute it.

terminal_shown: Mitochondrial complex I deficiency, nuclear type 27
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that FUT8-mediated core fucosylation of N-linked glycans on the NDUFAF6 assembly factor impairs its stability or mitochondrial import, disrupting assembly of mitochondrial complex I and contributing to mitochondrial complex I deficiency, nuclear type 27. NDUFAF6 is essential for early complex I assembly, and aberrant glycosylation could alter its conformation, interactions, or turnover. We predict that patient-derived cells with elevated FUT8 expression will show reduced NDUFAF6 protein levels and impaired complex I assembly, which will be rescued by FUT8 knockdown or inhibition. Conversely, loss of FUT8 should restore NDUFAF6 function and complex I activity. This hypothesis is falsifiable: detection of core fucosylation on NDUFAF6 via mass spectrometry and inverse correlation between FUT8 activity and NDUFAF6 stability would support it; absence of NDUFAF6 glycosylation or no effect of FUT8 modulation on complex I function would refute it.

terminal_shown: Hereditary leiomyomatosis and renal cell cancer
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that mutations in ATP6V1A, a subunit of the vacuolar H+-ATPase complex, impair lysosomal acidification, leading to defective degradation of the oncoprotein HIF-1α in cells with fumarate hydratase (FH) deficiency—a hallmark of hereditary leiomyomatosis and renal cell cancer (HLRCC). In HLRCC, FH loss causes fumarate accumulation, which inhibits prolyl hydroxylases (PHDs), stabilizing HIF-1α. We propose that ATP6V1A dysfunction exacerbates HIF-1α stabilization by compromising lysosomal turnover of HIF-1α, synergizing with fumarate-driven inhibition of PHDs. Prediction: In FH-deficient renal epithelial cells, CRISPR-mediated ATP6V1A knockdown will further increase HIF-1α protein levels and enhance hypoxia-responsive gene expression (e.g., VEGF, GLUT1) under normoxia. This effect will be reversed by reconstituting wild-type ATP6V1A, but not by a proton-pumping-deficient mutant. Refutation: If ATP6V1A loss does not further elevate HIF-1α in FH-null cells beyond fumarate accumulation alone, the hypothesis is invalidated.

We hypothesize that ALG11, an α-1,2-mannosyltransferase essential for N-linked glycan biosynthesis, contributes to Hypotrichosis 4 through defective glycosylation of hair keratin-associated proteins (KRTAPs). Impaired ALG11 activity disrupts the synthesis of the lipid-linked oligosaccharide precursor (Glc₃Man₉GlcNAc₂), leading to incomplete N-glycosylation of KRTAPs in the endoplasmic reticulum. Misfolded or hypoglycosylated KRTAPs trigger ER stress and unfolded protein response activation in hair follicle keratinocytes, disrupting hair shaft integrity and cycling. We predict that patient-derived keratinocytes with ALG11 mutations will exhibit reduced Man₉GlcNAc₂-PP-dolichol levels and increased BiP/CHOP expression, reversible by wild-type ALG11 expression. Conversely, normal glycosylation patterns and absence of ER stress markers in ALG11-mutant cells would refute this mechanism. This hypothesis links ALG11’s canonical role in N-glycosylation directly to the pathogenesis of Hypotrichosis 4 via disrupted structural protein maturation in hair follicles.

We hypothesize that CYP4F8, an enzyme involved in the ω-hydroxylation of arachidonic acid and inactivation of anti-inflammatory epoxyeicosatrienoic acids (EETs), modulates B-cell class-switch recombination by altering EET-mediated NF-κB signaling. In Immunodeficiency with hyper-IgM 2 (HIGM2), caused by mutations in *UNG* impairing Ig class switching, dysregulated CYP4F8 activity may exacerbate the phenotype by prematurely degrading EETs, which normally suppress aberrant NF-κB activation and support B-cell tolerance. We predict that CYP4F8 overexpression in *UNG*-deficient B cells will reduce EET levels, increase NF-κB-driven CD40-independent IgM production, and further suppress IgG/IgA switching. Conversely, CYP4F8 inhibition should elevate EETs, dampen NF-κB signaling, and partially restore class switching. This hypothesis is falsifiable: measuring IgG/IgA in *UNG*−/− B cells treated with a CYP4F8 inhibitor (e.g., HET0016) will show increased switching if the hypothesis is correct; no change or decreased switching would refute it.

We hypothesize that ARAF kinase hyperactivation disrupts insulin signaling in adipocytes by aberrantly phosphorylating insulin receptor substrate 1 (IRS1) on inhibitory serine residues (e.g., Ser636/639), impairing adipogenesis and promoting lipodystrophy in congenital generalized lipodystrophy type 5 (CGL5). This dysregulation arises from ARAF overexpression or gain-of-function mutations that enhance its kinase activity, leading to sustained ERK1/2 pathway activation and feedback inhibition of insulin signaling. We predict that knockdown or pharmacological inhibition of ARAF in CGL5 patient-derived preadipocytes will restore IRS1 tyrosine phosphorylation, enhance AKT activation, and rescue adipocyte differentiation, as measured by lipid accumulation and PPARγ expression. Conversely, overexpression of constitutively active ARAF in wild-type preadipocytes should recapitulate the CGL5 phenotype. Failure to restore insulin signaling or adipogenesis upon ARAF inhibition would refute this hypothesis.

We hypothesize that BAK1 (Bcl-2 homologous antagonist/killer 1) promotes excessive apoptosis in chondrocytes by amplifying mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization during endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress, exacerbating the pathogenesis of Chondrodysplasia punctata 2, X-linked dominant (CDPX2), which results from mutations in EBP (emopamil binding protein) involved in cholesterol biosynthesis. Impaired cholesterol synthesis in CDPX2 leads to toxic sterol intermediate accumulation and chronic ER stress; we propose that BAK1 hyperactivation under these conditions sensitizes chondrocytes to apoptosis, disrupting growth plate organization and causing stippled epiphyses. Prediction: In a CDPX2 cellular model (e.g., EBP-mutant chondrocytes), BAK1 knockdown or inhibition will reduce cytochrome c release, caspase-3 activation, and apoptotic cell death during ER stress. Conversely, BAK1 overexpression will exacerbate apoptosis. Refutation: If BAK1 modulation shows no effect on apoptosis in EBP-deficient chondrocytes under ER stress, the hypothesis is invalidated.

We hypothesize that ATP5MC1 deficiency impairs the assembly or stability of the mitochondrial ATP synthase complex, leading to chronic mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) instability, which in turn disrupts the import and retention of nuclear-encoded factors essential for mtDNA replication and maintenance, thereby causing mtDNA depletion in Mitochondrial DNA depletion syndrome 21 (MTDPS21). Specifically, loss-of-function mutations in ATP5MC1 compromise the c-subunit ring of ATP synthase, reducing proton flux and Δψm, which we predict will decrease the import of Twinkle helicase and POLG into the mitochondrial matrix. We predict that patient-derived fibroblasts with biallelic ATP5MC1 mutations will show reduced mtDNA copy number, diminished Twinkle and POLG mitochondrial levels, and rescued mtDNA content upon lentiviral expression of wild-type ATP5MC1. Failure to rescue mtDNA levels would refute this mechanism.

We hypothesize that malic enzyme 3 (ME3), localized in the mitochondrial matrix, contributes to Cataract 44 by disrupting redox homeostasis in lens epithelial cells through altered NADPH/NADP+ ratios. ME3 catalyzes the oxidative decarboxylation of malate to pyruvate, generating NADPH. Overactivity or dysregulation of ME3 may deplete mitochondrial malate, perturb the malate-aspartate shuttle, and reduce cytosolic NADPH availability—compromising glutathione reductase activity and increasing oxidative stress in the lens. We predict that *ME3* gain-of-function mutations in model systems will decrease reduced glutathione levels and increase protein aggregation in lens fibers, accelerating cataract formation. Conversely, *ME3* knockdown or inhibition will restore redox balance and delay cataract onset. This hypothesis is falsifiable: if ME3 modulation shows no effect on lens redox state or opacity in *in vivo* models of Cataract 44, the proposed mechanism is invalidated.

We hypothesize that MDM2, an E3 ubiquitin ligase, contributes to the pathogenesis of Congenital Disorder of Glycosylation 1H (CDG1H) by promoting the ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation of ALG1, the defective enzyme in CDG1H due to ALG1 gene mutations. MDM2 may recognize hypoglycosylated or misfolded ALG1 as a substrate under endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress, accelerating its turnover and further reducing already compromised ALG1 activity required for early steps in lipid-linked oligosaccharide assembly. We predict that pharmacological inhibition or genetic knockdown of MDM2 in CDG1H patient fibroblasts will increase ALG1 protein levels and restore N-glycosylation efficiency, as measured by improved LLO intermediates and transferrin glycosylation patterns. Conversely, MDM2 overexpression should exacerbate ALG1 deficiency and glycosylation defects. This hypothesis is falsifiable: failure of MDM2 modulation to alter ALG1 stability or glycosylation outcomes would refute a functional role for MDM2 in CDG1H pathophysiology.

We hypothesize that dysfunction of the mitochondrial complex I subunit ND2 impairs the proton gradient necessary for aspartate export from mitochondria via the glutamate-aspartate carrier (SLC25A12), reducing cytosolic aspartate availability for N-acetylaspartate (NAA) synthesis by NAT8L in neurons. Since NAA is synthesized in neurons from acetyl-CoA and aspartate, ND2 defects—by disrupting oxidative phosphorylation and mitochondrial membrane potential—would indirectly limit aspartate efflux, leading to decreased NAA production and manifesting as N-acetylaspartate deficiency. We predict that neurons derived from ND2-mutant mitochondrial disease models will show reduced aspartate levels, diminished NAA synthesis, and impaired SLC25A12 activity, which can be rescued by supplementation with membrane-permeable aspartate esters. Conversely, if aspartate levels and NAA synthesis remain normal in these neurons, or if NAA deficiency persists despite aspartate restoration, the hypothesis is refuted. This mechanism links mitochondrial bioenergetics directly to NAA biosynthesis through substrate availability.

We hypothesize that mutations in COX8A impair mitochondrial complex IV assembly or activity, leading to defective oxidative phosphorylation in chondrocytes, which disrupts energy-dependent endochondral ossification and causes the rhizomelic skeletal abnormalities characteristic of Rhizomelic dysplasia, Ain-Naz type. Specifically, loss-of-function variants in COX8A may destabilize the cytochrome c oxidase complex, reducing ATP production and increasing reactive oxygen species in growth plate cartilage. This metabolic stress would impair chondrocyte proliferation and matrix mineralization, directly contributing to shortened proximal limbs. We predict that patient-derived chondrocytes with COX8A mutations will show reduced complex IV activity, diminished oxygen consumption rates, and aberrant extracellular matrix deposition compared to controls—results that would confirm the hypothesis. Conversely, normal complex IV function and mitochondrial respiration in these cells would refute it.

We hypothesize that hyperactive PRKACA (cAMP-dependent protein kinase catalytic subunit alpha) disrupts RNA processing in developing neurons by aberrantly phosphorylating components of the tRNA splicing endonuclease complex, exacerbating the molecular pathology of Pontocerebellar hypoplasia 12 (PCH12), which is caused by mutations in the *TSEN54* gene. Specifically, PRKACA-mediated phosphorylation of residual functional TSEN complex subunits may further impair tRNA splicing, leading to accumulation of unspliced tRNAs and consequent translational deficiency in pontocerebellar neurons. We predict that inhibiting PRKACA activity in *TSEN54*-mutant human cerebellar organoids will restore tRNA splicing efficiency and improve neuronal survival (confirmation), whereas PRKACA overexpression will worsen splicing defects and neurodegeneration (refutation). This hypothesis is grounded in PRKACA’s known role in phosphorylating serine residues on nuclear substrates and the established link between tRNA splicing failure and PCH12 neuropathology.
