We propose that upregulated CYP11B2 activity in adrenal glomerulosa cells leads to elevated circulating 18-hydroxycorticosterone, which binds the mineralocorticoid receptor in proximal tubules and stimulates NADPH oxidase, worsening oxidative damage and impairing reabsorptive function. Prediction: In *Slc34a1*-knockout mice, genetic ablation or pharmacological inhibition of CYP11B2 will reduce renal oxidative stress markers (e.g., 8-OHdG, NOX4) and improve proximal tubule reabsorption (measured by urinary glucose, phosphate, and bicarbonate). Conversely, overexpression of CYP11B2 will worsen tubular dysfunction. This hypothesis is falsifiable by observing no improvement in tubular function despite CYP11B2 inhibition.

terminal_shown: Neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly, impaired language, and gait abnormalities
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that FDPS (farnesyl diphosphate synthase) deficiency disrupts protein prenylation in neural progenitor cells, impairing Ras and related GTPase signaling, leading to aberrant neurogenesis and cortical development. Reduced FDPS activity decreases farnesyl pyrophosphate production, limiting post-translational modification of small GTPases critical for neuronal proliferation, migration, and synapse formation. This dysregulation contributes to microcephaly, impaired language, and gait abnormalities via disrupted corticospinal and language network circuitry. We predict that patient-derived iPSC neurons with FDPS loss-of-function mutations will show reduced farnesylation of HRAS and impaired neurite outgrowth, reversible by supplementation with farnesol (a metabolic precursor). Conversely, if neurite defects persist despite farnesol treatment or if farnesylated HRAS levels remain normal in mutant neurons, the hypothesis will be refuted. This mechanism specifically links FDPS-dependent prenylation to neurodevelopmental deficits characteristic of the disorder.

We hypothesize that PLPP1 (pyridoxal phosphate phosphatase 1) deficiency impairs mitochondrial pyridoxal 5'-phosphate (PLP) availability, reducing functional aminolevulinic acid synthase 2 (ALAS2) activity in erythroid precursors, thereby causing pathological iron accumulation and ineffective erythropoiesis in Anemia, sideroblastic, 1. PLPP1 dephosphorylates PLP to pyridoxal, facilitating its cellular export or subcellular trafficking; loss of PLPP1 function may paradoxically trap PLP in compartments inaccessible to ALAS2, which requires PLP as a cofactor for heme biosynthesis. We predict that PLPP1 knockdown in human CD34+ derived erythroblasts will decrease ALAS2 activity, increase mitochondrial iron, and impair heme synthesis—phenocopying ALAS2 mutations. Conversely, restoring compartment-specific PLP availability via targeted PLP transporters should rescue heme production. These results would confirm the hypothesis; absence of heme deficiency or mitochondrial iron loading despite PLPP1 loss would refute it.

We hypothesize that impaired ICMT (isoprenylcysteine carboxyl methyltransferase) activity disrupts the methylation of prenylated proteins in hepatocytes, leading to aberrant subcellular localization of signaling proteins that regulate GNMT (Glycine N-methyltransferase) expression, thereby exacerbating hepatic methylome instability in Glycine N-methyltransferase deficiency. Specifically, reduced ICMT-mediated methylation of RAB GTPases may impair GNMT vesicular trafficking or stability, diminishing residual GNMT function in deficient states. We predict that hepatocyte-specific Icmt knockout in a Gnmt−/− mouse model will show significantly reduced GNMT protein (but not mRNA) levels and worsened S-adenosylmethionine accumulation compared to Gnmt−/− controls. Conversely, overexpression of ICMT in this background will restore GNMT protein levels and partially normalize methyl donor metabolites. Failure to observe these changes would refute the hypothesis.

We hypothesize that MOGAT1 (monoacylglycerol O-acyltransferase 1) contributes to aberrant lipid droplet dynamics in peripheral nerve axons by increasing diacylglycerol (DAG) and triacylglycerol (TAG) synthesis from monoacylglycerol, thereby disrupting endoplasmic reticulum (ER) membrane homeostasis and impairing mitochondrial trafficking in *GARS1*-mutant neurons associated with Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, axonal, type 2D. Elevated MOGAT1 activity is predicted to exacerbate lipid-induced ER stress and alter membrane curvature at ER-mitochondria contact sites, worsening axonal degeneration. Inhibition of MOGAT1 in *GARS1*-mutant human iPSC-derived motor neurons will restore mitochondrial transport velocity and reduce lipid droplet accumulation (confirmation), whereas MOGAT1 overexpression will further impair transport and increase stress markers (refutation if no change or improvement occurs). This prediction is testable via live imaging and lipidomic profiling.

We hypothesize that B3GNT3 promotes esophageal cancer progression by synthesizing poly-N-acetyllactosamine (poly-LacNAc) chains on β1-integrins, enhancing integrin clustering and focal adhesion kinase (FAK) signaling, thereby increasing tumor cell adhesion, migration, and invasion. In esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC), elevated B3GNT3 expression correlates with advanced stage and poor prognosis. We predict that CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knockout of B3GNT3 in ESCC cell lines will reduce poly-LacNAc modification of β1-integrin, decrease FAK phosphorylation (Tyr397), and impair cell migration in transwell assays. Conversely, overexpression of B3GNT3 will enhance these phenotypes. Immunoprecipitation followed by lectin blotting with Erythrina cristagalli lectin (ECL) will confirm reduced poly-LacNAc in knockout cells. This hypothesis is falsifiable: if B3GNT3 knockout fails to alter integrin glycosylation, FAK activation, or cell motility in ESCC models, the proposed mechanism is invalidated.

We hypothesize that reduced activity of phosphatidylinositol 4-kinase alpha (PI4KA) impairs endosomal trafficking and lysosomal delivery of heparan sulfate in neuronal cells, exacerbating substrate accumulation in Mucopolysaccharidosis 3A (MPS IIIA). PI4KA generates phosphatidylinositol 4-phosphate (PI4P), a lipid essential for Golgi-to-endosome vesicular transport and lysosomal positioning. In MPS IIIA, deficient sulfamidase leads to heparan sulfate buildup; we propose that concomitant PI4KA dysfunction further disrupts lysosomal clearance by mislocalizing key trafficking proteins (e.g., Rab7, VPS26), trapping heparan sulfate in swollen endosomes. Prediction: In *in vitro* models of MPS IIIA, pharmacological activation of PI4KA will restore lysosomal heparan sulfate degradation and normalize endosomal morphology, whereas PI4KA inhibition will worsen accumulation. This will be confirmed by reduced heparan sulfate levels and improved lysosomal function upon PI4KA activation (measured via LC-MS/MS and LysoTracker), and refuted if no change occurs despite PI4P level modulation.

We hypothesize that IMPA1 (inositol monophosphatase 1) deficiency exacerbates endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress in Cystathionine beta-synthase (CBS) deficiency by impairing inositol recycling and reducing free inositol levels, thereby compromising the phosphatidylinositol cycle and ER homeostasis. In CBS deficiency, homocysteine accumulation already disrupts protein folding and induces ER stress; diminished IMPA1 activity further limits inositol availability, weakening the unfolded protein response (UPR) and increasing cellular vulnerability. We predict that fibroblasts from CBS-deficient patients with pharmacological or genetic IMPA1 inhibition will show significantly elevated levels of ER stress markers (e.g., CHOP, BiP) and reduced cell viability compared to CBS-deficient cells with normal IMPA1 function. Conversely, exogenous inositol supplementation will rescue this phenotype. Failure to observe increased ER stress or rescue with inositol would refute the hypothesis. This mechanism links IMPA1’s role in inositol metabolism directly to the pathophysiology of CBS deficiency.

We hypothesize that RETSAT (retinol saturase) exacerbates porphyria-related encephalopathy by disrupting heme biosynthesis through aberrant retinoid metabolism. RETSAT catalyzes the saturation of all-trans-retinol to 13,14-dihydroretinol, which may competitively inhibit 5-aminolevulinate synthase (ALAS1), the rate-limiting enzyme in hepatic heme production. In porphyria, where heme synthesis is already impaired, RETSAT upregulation could further reduce heme availability, increasing accumulation of neurotoxic porphyrin precursors like ALA and PBG, thereby promoting encephalopathy. We predict that *RetSat*-knockout mice subjected to a porphyrogenic diet (e.g., phenobarbital or 3-methylcholanthrene) will exhibit lower ALA/PBG levels, reduced neurologic symptoms, and preserved ALAS1 activity compared to wild-type controls. Conversely, RETSAT overexpression should worsen these outcomes. These results would confirm RETSAT’s role in modulating heme pathway flux during porphyria; absence of such effects would refute the hypothesis.

We hypothesize that AKR1C8 impairs mitochondrial nucleotide homeostasis by reducing intramitochondrial dNTP pools through aberrant metabolism of deoxycytidine, exacerbating TK2 deficiency in Mitochondrial DNA Depletion Syndrome 2 (MDS2). Specifically, AKR1C8 may catalyze the NADPH-dependent reduction of deoxycytidine to inactive dihydrodeoxycytidine, diverting it from phosphorylation by TK2 and limiting dCTP availability for mtDNA synthesis. In MDS2, where TK2 activity is already compromised, overexpression or mislocalization of AKR1C8 to mitochondria would further restrict dNTP pools, accelerating mtDNA depletion. We predict that siRNA knockdown of AKR1C8 in TK2-deficient patient fibroblasts will restore mtDNA copy number and dCTP levels (confirming the hypothesis), whereas overexpression of mitochondrial-targeted AKR1C8 will worsen mtDNA depletion (refuting it if no change occurs). This mechanism is grounded in AKR1C8’s known reductase activity toward nucleoside analogs and the established dNTP insufficiency in MDS2.

We hypothesize that retinitis pigmentosa 73 (RP73), caused by mutations in *SLC33A1*, is exacerbated by dysregulated O-acetylation of sialic acids due to impaired acetyl-CoA transport into the endoplasmic reticulum, where the SLC33A1 transporter normally supplies acetyl-CoA to the acetyltransferase CASD1 (source enzyme: 107987478). Loss-of-function mutations in SLC33A1 reduce acetyl-CoA availability, diminishing CASD1-mediated sialic acid acetylation. This disrupts ganglioside composition in photoreceptor cell membranes, impairing disc morphogenesis and increasing oxidative stress susceptibility. We predict that patient-derived retinal organoids with *SLC33A1* mutations will show reduced sialic acid O-acetylation and mislocalization of rhodopsin, which will be rescued by expression of wild-type SLC33A1 but not by acetyl-CoA-binding-deficient mutants. Conversely, absence of these defects in *SLC33A1*-mutant organoids would refute the hypothesis.

terminal_shown: Hyperornithinemia with gyrate atrophy of choroid and retina
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that CYP2W1 metabolizes ornithine or a related polyamine in the retina, generating toxic byproducts that exacerbate mitochondrial dysfunction in individuals with hyperornithinemia due to ornithine aminotransferase (OAT) deficiency. Normally, OAT deficiency leads to ornithine accumulation, but we propose that CYP2W1—expressed ectopically in retinal pigment epithelium—oxidizes excess ornithine or downstream polyamines (e.g., putrescine), producing reactive aldehydes or oxidative stress that accelerate chorioretinal atrophy. Inhibition of CYP2W1 will reduce cytotoxic metabolite formation and preserve retinal structure. Prediction: In OAT-deficient human retinal organoids, CYP2W1 knockdown will decrease markers of oxidative stress (e.g., 4-HNE) and apoptosis (e.g., caspase-3), improving cell survival; conversely, CYP2W1 overexpression will worsen these outcomes. Refutation: If CYP2W1 modulation shows no effect on ornithine-associated toxicity in this context, the hypothesis is invalidated.

We hypothesize that ATP6V1FP2, a subunit of the vacuolar H⁺-ATPase complex, disrupts endosomal acidification in developing renal tubular epithelial cells, impairing the proteolytic activation of prorenin and subsequent renin-angiotensin system (RAS) signaling essential for renal tubulogenesis. Loss-of-function mutations in ATP6V1FP2 compromise V-ATPase assembly or activity, leading to defective acidification of endosomes, which is required for cathepsin-mediated cleavage of prorenin into active renin. This results in local RAS deficiency during nephrogenesis, contributing to the arrested differentiation of proximal tubules characteristic of renal tubular dysgenesis. We predict that patient-derived renal epithelial cells with ATP6V1FP2 mutations will exhibit elevated endosomal pH, reduced active renin, and diminished angiotensin II production; these defects would be rescued by expression of wild-type ATP6V1FP2. Conversely, absence of these biochemical changes despite mutation would refute the hypothesis.

We hypothesize that PLA2G4B, a calcium-dependent cytosolic phospholipase A2-beta, impairs mitochondrial nucleotide homeostasis by aberrantly hydrolyzing cardiolipin in the inner mitochondrial membrane, leading to reduced dNTP import and subsequent mtDNA depletion in Mitochondrial DNA Depletion Syndrome 2 (MNGIE-like phenotype due to *TYMP* mutations). Chronic PLA2G4B overactivity increases lysocardiolipin and free fatty acid accumulation, disrupting mitochondrial membrane potential required for the TIM/TOM-mediated import of thymidine kinase 2 (TK2) and deoxyribonucleotide transporters. We predict that siRNA-mediated knockdown of *PLA2G4B* in *TYMP*-deficient fibroblasts will restore cardiolipin levels, improve mtDNA copy number, and normalize mitochondrial respiration. Conversely, overexpression of wild-type PLA2G4B in these cells will exacerbate mtDNA depletion. These results would confirm or refute PLA2G4B’s role in modulating mtDNA stability via cardiolipin metabolism in MNGIE pathophysiology.

We hypothesize that NAT2 (N-acetyltransferase 2) modulates the acetylation state of fumarase (fumarate hydratase), thereby influencing its stability or catalytic activity in the mitochondrial matrix. In Fumarase deficiency, loss-of-function mutations in *FH* lead to fumarate accumulation and impaired TCA cycle flux. We propose that NAT2-mediated lysine acetylation of fumarase promotes its degradation or inactivation, exacerbating the metabolic consequences of partial *FH* mutations. Specifically, we predict that *NAT2* knockout in a human *FH* heterozygous cell line will increase fumarase protein levels and activity, reduce fumarate accumulation, and restore ATP production compared to *NAT2*-wildtype controls. Conversely, NAT2 overexpression will further reduce fumarase activity and worsen metabolic phenotypes. This hypothesis is falsifiable: if NAT2 knockout fails to increase fumarase activity or fumarate levels remain elevated, the proposed regulatory mechanism is unsupported. The link relies on established roles of lysine acetylation in regulating mitochondrial enzymes.

We hypothesize that reduced A4GALT (alpha-1,4-galactosyltransferase) activity disrupts glycosphingolipid biosynthesis in lens fiber cells, leading to aberrant membrane microdomain organization and impaired lens transparency in Cataract 38. Specifically, diminished synthesis of the Pk blood group antigen (Galα1-4Galβ1-4Glc-ceramide) due to A4GALT deficiency destabilizes lipid rafts, perturbing the localization and function of gap junction proteins such as connexin 50. This disruption compromises intercellular communication and lens homeostasis, promoting protein aggregation and light scattering. We predict that A4GALT-knockdown human lens epithelial cells will exhibit reduced Pk antigen levels, mislocalized connexin 50, and increased intracellular light scatter, measurable by flow cytometry and confocal microscopy. Conversely, overexpression of wild-type A4GALT will restore Pk expression, normalize connexin 50 distribution, and reduce scatter. These results would confirm the hypothesis; absence of these effects despite A4GALT modulation would refute it.

We hypothesize that HRAS activation promotes tyrosine accumulation in Tyrosinemia 3 by upregulating phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH) expression via the RAF-MEK-ERK signaling cascade, increasing phenylalanine-to-tyrosine conversion. In Tyrosinemia 3, caused by HPD deficiency, this excess tyrosine cannot be efficiently metabolized to homogentisate, exacerbating metabolic blockage. We predict that in *Hras*-knockdown hepatocyte models with *Hpd* silencing, tyrosine levels will be significantly lower than in *Hpd*-deficient controls with intact HRAS (confirmation). Conversely, constitutive HRAS activation in *Hpd*-deficient cells will further elevate intracellular tyrosine (support). The hypothesis is refuted if HRAS modulation shows no effect on tyrosine concentration in *Hpd*-deficient systems, despite pathway activation. This mechanism is plausible given HRAS’s role in regulating hepatic metabolic gene expression through MAPK signaling, directly linking dysregulated growth signaling to tyrosine homeostasis disruption specific to Tyrosinemia 3.

We hypothesize that δ-aminolevulinic acid dehydratase (ALAD) exacerbates iron accumulation in Hemochromatosis 5 (due to FTH1 mutations) by increasing labile heme synthesis, which disrupts iron sensing in hepatocytes. In FTH1 deficiency, impaired ferritin iron sequestration elevates cytosolic iron. ALAD, by condensing two δ-aminolevulinic acid molecules into porphobilinogen, drives heme biosynthesis. Excess heme may downregulate ferroportin and upregulate hepcidin via BMP6 signaling, further restricting iron export. We predict that ALAD inhibition in FTH1-mutant hepatocytes will reduce intracellular heme, normalize hepcidin expression, and decrease iron retention. Conversely, ALAD overexpression will worsen iron accumulation. This would be confirmed by reduced iron and hepcidin levels upon ALAD knockdown in FTH1-deficient human hepatoma cells; refuted if iron levels remain unchanged despite ALAD modulation. The mechanism specifically links heme flux to iron dysregulation in Hemochromatosis 5.

terminal_shown: Maturity-onset diabetes of the young 8 with exocrine dysfunction
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that B3GALT2 deficiency disrupts β1,3-galactosyltransferase-mediated glycosylation of N-glycans in pancreatic progenitor cells, impairing Notch receptor trafficking and signaling during pancreatic development. This defect leads to aberrant differentiation of endocrine and exocrine lineages, reducing β-cell mass and acinar cell function, thereby causing Maturity-onset diabetes of the young 8 with exocrine dysfunction. Specifically, loss of B3GALT2-mediated galactosylation of N-acetylglucosamine residues on Notch extracellular domain EGF repeats reduces ligand-induced activation, diminishing Hes1 expression. We predict that B3GALT2-knockout human pancreatic organoids will show reduced insulin+ cells and digestive enzyme-producing acinar cells, with rescue upon re-expression of wild-type B3GALT2 but not catalytically inactive mutants. Conversely, preserved Notch signaling and cell differentiation in heterozygous carriers would refute a haploinsufficiency mechanism. This hypothesis links B3GALT2’s glycosyltransferase activity directly to developmental pathogenesis specific to this monogenic diabetes-exocrine disorder.

We hypothesize that mutations in FKRP (fukutin-related protein) disrupt the ribitol-5-phosphate transfer required for dystroglycan O-mannosyl glycan elongation, leading to defective α-dystroglycan ligand binding in neuronal and glial cells, thereby compromising cortical lamination and blood-brain barrier integrity during development. This aberrant glycosylation impairs synaptic stability and increases neuronal hyperexcitability, contributing to the early-onset seizures and developmental regression characteristic of Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy 50 (DEE50). Specifically, we predict that patient-derived FKRP mutations will reduce incorporation of ribitol-5-phosphate into α-dystroglycan in induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived neurons, correlating with increased susceptibility to kainate-induced seizure-like activity in cortical organoids. This hypothesis would be confirmed by demonstrating rescued glycosylation and reduced hyperexcitability upon expression of wild-type FKRP, and refuted if FKRP mutations show normal glycosylation yet still cause hyperexcitability.

We hypothesize that mutations or dysregulation in CDS1 (CDP-diacylglycerol synthase 1) impair phosphatidylinositol (PI) biosynthesis in hair follicle stem cells, disrupting phosphoinositide signaling essential for follicular development and immune privilege maintenance, thereby contributing to Alopecia universalis congenita. Reduced CDS1 activity would decrease CDP-diacylglycerol availability for PI synthesis, compromising downstream PIP3-dependent AKT activation and promoting premature apoptosis or immune infiltration in the follicle. We predict that CDS1-deficient human scalp-derived keratinocytes or organoids will exhibit diminished PI(4,5)P2 and PIP3 levels, aberrant AKT phosphorylation, and upregulated IFN-γ response genes—effects rescued by exogenous PI supplementation. Conversely, normal phosphoinositide profiles and signaling in CDS1-mutant cells would refute this mechanism. This hypothesis is grounded in CDS1’s established role in phospholipid metabolism and the known sensitivity of hair follicle cycling to PI3K/AKT signaling and immune dysregulation, specifically linking CDS1 dysfunction to the congenital, total hair loss phenotype of Alopecia universalis.

We hypothesize that ASAH1, acid ceramidase, modulates N-glycosylation fidelity in Congenital Disorder of Glycosylation 1Q (CDG-IQ) by regulating ceramide levels that influence the Golgi pH and stability of the oligosaccharyltransferase (OST) complex, whose subunit DPM1 is mutated in CDG-IQ. Elevated ceramide due to ASAH1 deficiency acidifies the Golgi via increased proton influx, disrupting OST-mediated glycan transfer to proteins. We predict that fibroblasts from CDG-IQ patients with reduced ASAH1 activity will exhibit exacerbated hypoglycosylation of transferrin and increased ceramide accumulation, which can be rescued by ASAH1 overexpression or ceramide-lowering agents (e.g., myriocin). Conversely, restoring ASAH1 activity in CDG-IQ models should normalize Golgi pH, improve OST function, and rescue glycosylation defects. Falsification would occur if modulating ASAH1 or ceramide levels fails to alter glycosylation status in CDG-IQ cells despite confirmed biochemical changes in sphingolipid metabolism.

We hypothesize that monoamine oxidase A (MAOA) exacerbates oxidative stress in red blood cells by increasing hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) production during amine neurotransmitter catabolism, thereby worsening hemolysis in congenital non-spherocytic hemolytic anemia type 3 (CNSHA3), which results from glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency. In G6PD-deficient erythrocytes, diminished NADPH impairs glutathione reductase activity, weakening antioxidant defense. MAOA-derived H₂O₂ would further overwhelm this compromised system, promoting hemoglobin oxidation and membrane damage. We predict that pharmacological inhibition of MAOA in G6PD-deficient human erythrocytes exposed to serotonin will reduce H₂O₂ accumulation and hemolysis compared to controls (confirmation); conversely, no reduction in hemolysis with MAOA inhibition would refute the hypothesis. This mechanism specifically links MAOA activity to oxidative hemolysis in CNSHA3, independent of spherocyte formation.

We hypothesize that deficient activity of medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (ACADM) leads to accumulation of medium-chain fatty acids and their toxic metabolites, impairing mitochondrial function in autonomic neurons and contributing to the pathogenesis of visceral neuropathy, familial, 1, autosomal recessive. Specifically, we propose that ACADM deficiency causes chronic bioenergetic stress and oxidative damage in postganglionic visceral neurons due to incomplete fatty acid β-oxidation, disrupting axonal transport and neurotransmitter release. This mechanism is consistent with the disease’s autonomic dysfunction phenotype. We predict that patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) neurons with biallelic *ACADM* mutations will exhibit reduced ATP levels, increased reactive oxygen species, and impaired neurite outgrowth—phenotypes reversible with antioxidant treatment or medium-chain fatty acid restriction. Conversely, normal metabolic and neuronal function in such cells would refute our hypothesis.

We hypothesize that ATP6V1H deficiency impairs vacuolar H+-ATPase (V-ATPase)-mediated acidification of extracellular microvesicles secreted by vascular smooth muscle cells, reducing their capacity to dissolve calcium phosphate crystals, thereby promoting arterial calcification in Arterial Calcification of Infancy, Generalized, 2 (ACI2). ACI2 is caused by mutations in ENPP1, which generates pyrophosphate (PPi), a potent calcification inhibitor. We propose that ATP6V1H-dependent acidification is required for optimal activity of ENPP1 within microvesicles, where low pH stabilizes PPi and enhances its mineralization-inhibiting function. Prediction: In ATP6V1H-knockdown vascular cells, extracellular microvesicles will exhibit elevated intravesicular pH, reduced PPi levels, and increased hydroxyapatite deposition *in vitro*—phenocopying ENPP1 deficiency. Conversely, restoring ATP6V1H expression or artificially acidifying microvesicles will rescue PPi production and block calcification. Failure to observe altered microvesicle pH or PPi levels upon ATP6V1H modulation would refute this mechanism.

We hypothesize that GNPNAT1, by catalyzing the acetylation of D-glucosamine-6-phosphate in the hexosamine biosynthesis pathway (HBP), increases flux into O-GlcNAcylation of key signaling proteins in vascular smooth muscle cells, leading to enhanced vasoconstriction and elevated systemic vascular resistance in essential hypertension. Specifically, we propose that upregulated GNPNAT1 activity elevates UDP-GlcNAc levels, promoting O-GlcNAc modification of the myosin light chain phosphatase target subunit (MYPT1), thereby inhibiting phosphatase activity, increasing myosin light chain phosphorylation, and sustaining vascular tone. We predict that endothelial- and smooth muscle-specific *Gnpat1* knockout in hypertensive mouse models (e.g., SHR) will reduce arterial O-GlcNAcylation, lower blood pressure, and normalize vascular reactivity compared to controls. Conversely, overexpression of GNPNAT1 in vascular tissue will exacerbate hypertension. These outcomes would confirm or refute GNPNAT1’s mechanistic role in essential hypertension via HBP-driven vascular dysfunction.

We hypothesize that mutations in KDSR (3-ketodihydrosphingosine reductase) impair de novo sphingolipid biosynthesis, leading to aberrant mitochondrial membrane microdomain organization and disrupted assembly of oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) complexes I, III, and IV, thereby causing Combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency 35 (COXPD35). Specifically, KDSR deficiency reduces tetrahydroxy-2-keto-sphinganine production, altering cardiolipin-sphingolipid interactions essential for cristae morphology and supercomplex stability. We predict that fibroblasts from COXPD35 patients with biallelic KDSR mutations will show decreased complex I+III and III+IV supercomplexes via blue-native PAGE, which is rescued by expression of wild-type KDSR but not catalytically inactive KDSR (K202A). Conversely, normal supercomplex formation in KDSR-mutant cells would refute the hypothesis, as would absence of mitochondrial sphingolipid abnormalities on mass spectrometry. This mechanism directly links sphingolipid metabolism by KDSR to OXPHOS integrity, consistent with COXPD35’s molecular signature.
